The surface front was dragged north into Iowa by low pressure that moved out of Kansas northeast into central Iowa by the mid to late evening.  The airmass was pushed southeast out of the state by a cold front that passed through the state during the evening and early morning hours.  The airmass in the warm sector became very unstable.  Lifted indices were around -13 C with CAPE values greater than 5000 J/kg by the late afternoon.  The air advected north into Iowa during the day and into the evening.  Thunderstorms erupted in two places.  The first to affect the DSM CWA was the development of several elevated supercells over west central into southwest Iowa.  The storms continued to lift east and northeast across the area.  A few tornadoes touched down, however with the very elevated nature of the storms it was very difficult for the tornadoes to reach the ground.  By the late afternoon, a solid squall line developed along the cold front.  The line took on a Line Echo Wave Pattern by evening.  Several segments of the line bowed out, resulting in high winds.  At times the winds reached 80 MPH.  One of the thunderstorms produced high winds in the Early area of Sac County.  They overturned a semi-tractortrailer truck, causing $80,000 damage and causing minor injuries to the driver.  Tornadoes that formed along this line actually formed where the Rear Flank Downdraft cut through the line.  A clear meso was formed and the small tornadoes advanced around the meso and were in front of the thunderstorm line.  Touchdowns were all brief.  Hail was common with the stronger storm, with much of it in the one to one and three-quarter inch in diameter.  Given the antecedent soil conditions in Iowa, flash flooding became a major issue.  Numerous counties reported flash flooding as rainfall of one to 4 inches in spots resulted in flooded highways.  The thunderstorms formed into an MCC by the early evening hours.  As they moved out of the state, they delivered one more punch to the state.  High winds developed in the wake of the complex.  Several counties of north central, northeast, and central Iowa received high winds.  Damage occurred in several locations to both trees and out buildings.  Sustained winds across the area were in the 25 to 45 MPH range with some higher gusts.  Clarion reported a wind gust of 63 MPH for the highest wind gust reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm advection took place over Iowa during the late night hours of the 28th into the morning of the 29th.  A warm front was positioned to the south of Iowa, extending from southern Illinois into central Nebraska.  A 50 kt low level jet pushed over the top of the front and resulted in the formation of an MCS.  Most of the thunderstorms were not severe, however there were a few supercells embedded in the MCS which produced large hail.  Golf Ball size hail was reported in parts of Crawford and Sac Counties.  The storms initially produced high winds in Carroll County near Breda, totally destroying a barn.  As the night progressed, the storms took on more of a bow shape.  Several beta bow elements tracked east-southeast into western and central Iowa.  They produced winds of 60 to 65 MPH in a few locations.  High winds downed trees in the Pomeroy area of Calhoun County.  A machine shed was blown over south of Lidderdale in Carroll County.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter sized hail whitened the ground and removed leaves from the trees.
Nickel sized hail fell west of Cleveland. Golf ball sized hail was reported in the western portion of Le Sueur County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain that fell between 10 PM CDT on the 29th and 3 AM on the 30th caused widespread flooding of roads, fields, and waterways across Redwood and southern Renville counties.  In Renville County, portions of County Road 15 along the Minnesota River near between Franklin and Fairfax were severely eroded.  A mudslide was reported on County Road 15 near Morton. Several other ditches and gravel roads were eroded across the southern portion of the county.  Buffalo Creek nearly overflowed.  Portions of county roads 4 and 20 were closed by high water.   A total of 8 inches of rain was reported near Franklin.  In Redwood County, significant flooding was reported in Redwood Falls, Wabasso, and Morgan. Eight county roads had to be closed after water flowed over them. In Redwood Falls the Minnesota River crested 2 feet above flood stage.  The Redwood River, the Cottonwood River, and Ramsey Creek also ran high. Ramsey Park and the sway back bridge were closed by high water in addition to nearby County Road 31.  Numerous basements were flooded across the city.  In Morgan, many city residents reported flooded basements and nearby gravel roads were washed out. Farmers outside of town had to replant beans and corn after their fields flooded.  The highest rainfall totals included 8 inches in New Avon Township, 7 inches in Wabasso, and 5 inches in Redwood Falls.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A few large trees were downed onto a road.

In Green Lake County, a barn was blown down, and a tree fell on to a vehicle. Several rounds of thunderstorms during the April 20s caused periodic flash flooding over much of Madison County.  For the 72 hour period ending 7 am cdt April 24, Huntsville and St. Paul received 6.57 and 6.35 inches of rain respectively.  Numerous roads were flooded and as much as $100,000 damage was done to them.  Some homes in the Witter area were also flooded.  However; the most major event occured around 645 am cdt on the 24th.  A pickup truck containing 4 occupants stalled in high water over a bridge crossing Hock Creek 5 miles southwest of Huntsville.  A 3 year old girl and a 2 year old boy were swept away in the flood waters and died.  The woman driving the truck and another child escaped.On April 25th,  the governor of Arkansas declared Madison county a disaster area.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist, and unstable airmass was in place over Iowa.  The warm front that had produced the convection during the early morning hours of the 8th had become stationary over northern Iowa.  With lifted indices below -10 C. over central Iowa and continued strong moisture advection, thunderstorms erupted over the central and northeast parts of the state during the late afternoon and evening hours.  For the most part, the thunderstorms produced hail during this event.  There were numerous reports of hail of one to two inches in diameter.  Hail reportedly covered the ground in Guthrie County, into parts of Dallas County.  During the later evening hours, the thunderstorms began to sink south and took on a bow echo type configuration, though the line was not a true bow echo.  High winds began to be reported with Cass County being hit the worst.  A swath of damage 7 miles long was reported from west of Lewis to southeast of Lewis.  Embedded in the winds was a small tornado.  The tornado touched down intermittently along the 7 mile path and destroyed or damaged several grain bins and downed numerous trees.  A large corn crib was destroyed southeast of Atlantic and there were numerous reports of trees over highways.  In addition to the hail and high winds, heavy rain occurred from central into parts of west central Iowa.  Flash flooding occurred in Audubon, Guthrie, Madison, and Adair Counties.  Rain fell as the thunderstorms trained and redeveloped repeatedly over the same areas.  Rainfall rates were in the one to three inch per hour range with rainfall total reports of over 4 inches received in a few places in under two hours.  Water flooded over highways, even some U.S. Highways, to as depth of one to two feet.  This resulted in closure of some highways.
Flooding continued on mainly county roads in southern White County.
Street flooding was noted in and around Morrilton.
Water covered a few roads in Russellville.
Excessive rain flooded several low water crossings in Logan County.
Water covered several roads in Scott County, with a few low water crossings impassible.
Several roads were blocked or partially covered by water, including Highway 28 near Bluffton.
Excessive rain flooded several county roads in Perry County.
Some street flooding continued in Morrilton.

An upper level trough remained situated out to the west in Northern Mexico and the Southwest U.S.  A very unstable airmass developed during the afternoon hours across South Texas triggering thunderstorms.  An upper level shortwave rotated out of Mexico during the afternoon providing increasing large-scale ascent, divergence aloft and steepening mid-level lapse rates.  Thunderstorms initially began as supercells across the Rio Grande Plains and Duval and Jim Wells counties during the afternoon and early evening, producing large hail and heavy rain.  The supercells organized into a squall-line during the evening and moved east across the Coastal Bend, producing heavy rainfall and flash flooding.  A wake low formed over the Coastal Bend behind the squall line as it moved into the offshore waters during the late night and early morning hours.  High sustained winds of 40 to 50 mph, with some gusts over 60 mph, developed over the Coastal Bend, Victoria Crossroads region and the bays and nearshore waters.  Damage associated with these winds was mainly confined to tree limbs, however a tug boat in Port Oconnor was reportedly damaged.  See High Wind event entry as well as wind entries under Gulf of Mexico for further information.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful spring storm brought winter conditions to the Rocky Mountain Front and northern adjacent plains on the 11th. Snow and gusty winds began shortly after midnight and continued until late evening. Reported snow fall amounts include: 17 inches at Blackleaf  8WNW, 15 inches at Summit 2SE, 10 inches at Babb and 7 inches at Havre, Havre 25S, Cut Bank, Sweetgrass 25E, Chester 15N, and Valier.  Additionally, 24 inches of snow were estimated to have fallen at the SNOTEL site located at Badger Pass (Heart Butte 14SW). Damage from the heavy wet snow included downed tree limbs and several downed power lines in Glacier county. Slick roadways also accounted for numerous motor vehicle accidents.

A strong spring storm brought rain and snow to much of  North Central Montana from late on the 22nd through the early hours of the 24th. Heavy snow was reported at higher elevations while sites at lower elevations received heavy  rain. Reported snow fall amounts include: 12 inches near Kings Hill, 11 inches at the Lower Twin SNOTEL site, 11 inches at the Onion Park SNOTEL site, 11 inches at Lewistown 25SSE, 8 inches at Monida Pass, 8 inches at Neihart 8N, 7 inches at the Pike Creek and Lone Mountain SNOTEL sites and 6 inches at Wisdom 20W. Heavy rain fall reports for the storm event  include: 2.6 inches at Chinook 27S, 2.26 inches at Wolf Creek, 1.28 inches at Ulm 4S, 1.25 inches at Pendroy and 1.23 inches at Havre. The storm brought much needed moisture for area farmers as well as slick roadways.

A major late season winter storm affected a portion of northeast Montana beginning late on the evening of the 10th, and continued until about noon on the 12th. The storm produced up to a foot of heavy wet snow, with snow drifts up to 5 feet deep. Low pressure developed in Wyoming on the evening of the 10th and tracked into the Dakotas during the afternoon hours of the 11th. Rain changed to snow late on the evening of the 10th and during the pre dawn hours of the 11th.  Periods of snow continued through the morning of the 12th, and some of the snow fell heavily at times during the day on the 11th. Snowfall ranged from about 3 inches to as much as a foot across most of northeast Montana north of the Missouri River.  Snowdrifts of up to 5 feet were reported in northern Valley County. In addition, strong east winds of 20 to 40 mph produced considerable blowing and drifting snow which reduced the visibility to less than a quarter of a mile at times.  Many schools were closed, and roads were open to emergency travel only in Central and Northern Valley County as well as Daniels and Sheridan Counties during the day on the 11th and into the early morning hours of the 12th. Other thunderstorms developed over portions of east central Illinois and northwest Indiana. The major threat was heavy rain which produced widespread street flooding.  There were also reports of thunderstorm wind damage. A moist and unstable airmass was in place over Iowa during the afternoon of the 19th.  A southerly flow in the low levels brought dew point temperatures of the low 70s F. into southern Iowa. The airmass became capped over much of the state during the afternoon with a 2.4 degree C. cap in place over southwest Iowa by the early evening. It produced one and one half inch diameter hail as it passed southwest of Lakota in Kossuth County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very unstable airmass was over Iowa and helped kick off the seasons first severe weather outbreak.  At the surface a warm frontal boundary extended nearly east to west across the state and provided the focus for thunderstorm development.  By the late afternoon, lifted indices were approaching -10 C. with CAPE values around 5000 J/kg over western Iowa.  Surface temperatures warmed into the upper 80s with dew points in the low to mid 70s.  A southwest surface wind of 15 to 25 kts pushed over the front.  Northeast of the frontal boundary winds were easterly around 10 to 15 kts.  Actually, the surface boundary was further enhanced by outflow from convective complexes during the day, further sharpening the contrast.  Thunderstorms continued to fire along and north of the boundary through the afternoon and into the evening.  This resulted in widespread flash flooding as very heavy rains fell on areas that had had significant rainfall the previous night.  There were reports in north central into northeast Iowa of 2 to 4 inches of rainfall in a little more than an hours time.  Major flooding took place in the Mason City area where evacuations were taking place.  The thunderstorms became most intense during the afternoon into the early evening.  There were several tornadoes across northeast into north central Iowa.  Most were relatively brief touchdowns and were in open areas.  Reports of multi-vortex tornadoes were received from Grundy County.  The days most significant tornado touched down in Pocahontas County east of Rolfe and tracked into Humboldt County through the Bradgate area.  The tornado damaged or destroyed over 75% of the town of Bradgate (pop 120).  Tornado damage in Bradgate was very extensive impacting most of the town.  Hardly a building was not impacted.   Outbuildings, light structures and garages were heavily damaged or destroyed.  Two homes were destroyed.  Several homes were damaged ranging from minor to extensive.  The Survey Team found that the majority of the damage was F1, with a few cases of F2 damage.  The F2 damage was to the snapping of very large trees just west of town and the structural damage to two buildings.  Nearly all of the 53 homes there reported damage with several totally destroyed.  Significant widespread property damage was reported in the tornadoes path.  There were several injuries in the town, the most significant being a broken leg.  A police officer was reportedly hit by debris from the tornado and suffered a broken leg.  According to law officials, the damage path of the tornado was 2 miles wide and about 8 miles long.  Storm chasers on the scene reported the tornado itself to be one half mile wide at one point.  Reports of hail were numerous through the afternoon and evening.  Most of the hail was in the three quarter inch to one inch diameter range.  There were a few reports of golf ball size hail from the stronger storms.  Winds were not a major problem with the activity.  There were spotty reports of winds to around 60 MPH, but most reports were in the 40 to 50 MPH range.  One of the stronger wind reports was a 64 MPH wind gust in Tripoli in Bremer County.  This gust was measured by a mesonet station there.  During the mid evening hours, thunderstorms rumbled across Grundy County.  Lightning struck the Sheriff's office there and destroyed a significant amount of office equipment.  Damage was reported around $100,000.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tornado touched down in farm fields southwest of Dike.

A winter storm moving southeast from the Gulf of Alaska, picked up tropical moisture before it moved onshore. The warmer air mass caused the snow level to remain high during most of the precipitaion event, so that measured snow fall was less than eight inches in the mountains. The synoptic situation was very similar to what it was the previous day.  A complex weather situation was in place due to the convection from the previous night.  An outflow boundary extended east to west across northern Missouri.  The synoptic frontal boundary extended from central Nebraska across northern Iowa.  The air was clear over Iowa during the day, allowing for temperatures to recover.  Dew point values also recovered quite rapidly with readings in the upper 60s to low 70s by the late afternoon hours.  Lifted indices dropped into the -5 to -10 C. range by evening with CAPE values approaching 5000 J/kg.  By the evening hours, the frontal boundary and outflow boundary had converged and were located along Interstate 80.  Explosive thunderstorm development took place during the very late afternoon and evening hours in spite of the weak shear profile.  Discrete supercells formed in a narrow line along Interstate 80 from near Des Moines on west.  The storms became tornadic quickly.  To add insult to injury, a strong thunderstorm complex formed over Nebraska and moved east along the line of convection over Iowa.  As the event took shape, all modes of severe weather occurred.  The storms developed so rapidly that there was little more than a half hour from the first hail and wind report to the first tornado touchdown.  Hail and high wind reports were too numerous to mention individually here.  Numerous reports of golf ball size hail were received.  Boone and Story Counties reported some of the largest hail with the event as baseball size hail pelted the are.  There was one report of very large hail northwest of Slater in Story County.  Hail five and one half inches in diameter punched 8 holes through a steel roof.  There was severe house siding and roof damage in the area.  There were numerous tornadoes, especially in the central Iowa Iowa.  At one point there were several supercells around the metropolitan Des Moines area.  Two of the stronger tornadoes touched down west and south of Des Moines.  Fortunately, most of the tornado tracks were over open areas and resulted in little damage.  High winds became a problem, especially after sunset, as the complex from Nebraska moved in.  The system became more of a derecho during the late night hours.  Eighty plus MPH winds pelted southwest Iowa and downed barns and several buildings in Adams and Cass Counties.  A beta bow element formed in central Iowa shortly before midnight.  The bow echo produced a measured wind gust of 106 MPH in northern Warren County.  The high winds continued to push east along Interstate 80 for the next hour or so before it started to weaken.  The other major problem was with heavy rain.  The convection from the previous night set the stage by saturating soils.  The echos trained for several hours across central Iowa with very heavy rainfall.  Rainfall rates of 4 to 5 inches per hour were common under the heavier cells.  Several locations received 2 to 5 inch rainfalls in under  two hours, resulting in widespread flash flooding.  Reports of major highways being inundated by water were common.  By the end of the night, a swath of 4 to 9 inch rainfall was evident north of Interstate 80.  Longer term river flooding became a major problem by the morning of the 23rd.  There were two lightning related injuries.  Two people were injured when they were struck by lightning out of doors in Nevada.  The lightning struck close by as they were carrying groceries into their home.  The jolt caused them to fall, resulting in laceration to the head.

Several severe thunderstorms affected the northeast Permian Basin of west Texas during the late afternoon and evening of the 25th. These storms developed near a dryline/cold front triple point. A highly visible tornado was observed by many residents of Snyder in Scurry County. The parent thunderstorm produced large hail it tracked northeast over the city. A second supercell tracked east, then southeast across northern Mitchell County. This storm produced two tornadoes, baseball size hail, and damaging winds in the vicinity of Colorado City and Loraine.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado was observed by several Snyder residents to the southwest of the city. The tornado remained over open country west of U.S. Highway 350 and resulted in no damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Once again it was a very active severe weather day over Iowa.  The frontal system that had moved through the state on the night of the 22nd was returning north as a warm front.  This time Iowa did not get completely into the warm sector.  The surface front was dragged north into Iowa by low pressure that moved out of Kansas northeast into central Iowa by the mid to late evening.  The airmass was pushed southeast out of the state by a cold front that passed through the state during the evening and early morning hours.  The airmass in the warm sector became very unstable.  Lifted indices were around -13 C with CAPE values greater than 5000 J/kg by the late afternoon.  The air advected north into Iowa during the day and into the evening.  Thunderstorms erupted in two places.  The first to affect the DSM CWA was the development of several elevated supercells over west central into southwest Iowa.  The storms continued to lift east and northeast across the area.  A few tornadoes touched down, however with the very elevated nature of the storms it was very difficult for the tornadoes to reach the ground.  By the late afternoon, a solid squall line developed along the cold front.  The line took on a Line Echo Wave Pattern by evening.  Several segments of the line bowed out, resulting in high winds.  At times the winds reached 80 MPH.  One of the thunderstorms produced high winds in the Early area of Sac County.  They overturned a semi-tractortrailer truck, causing $80,000 damage and causing minor injuries to the driver.  Tornadoes that formed along this line actually formed where the Rear Flank Downdraft cut through the line.  A clear meso was formed and the small tornadoes advanced around the meso and were in front of the thunderstorm line.  Touchdowns were all brief.  Hail was common with the stronger storm, with much of it in the one to one and three-quarter inch in diameter.  Given the antecedent soil conditions in Iowa, flash flooding became a major issue.  Numerous counties reported flash flooding as rainfall of one to 4 inches in spots resulted in flooded highways.  The thunderstorms formed into an MCC by the early evening hours.  As they moved out of the state, they delivered one more punch to the state.  High winds developed in the wake of the complex.  Several counties of north central, northeast, and central Iowa received high winds.  Damage occurred in several locations to both trees and out buildings.  Sustained winds across the area were in the 25 to 45 MPH range with some higher gusts.  Clarion reported a wind gust of 63 MPH for the highest wind gust reported.

A strong push of moisture streamed into Iowa on a 50 to 70 kt low level jet.  Lifted indices were around -9 C at the beginning of the event with CAPE in the 2500 to 4000 J/kg range.  Thunderstorms erupted to the west and southwest of Iowa with the initial development being discrete supercells to the southwest, and linear ahead of an approaching cold front to the west.  The storms became much more multi-cellular as they moved into Iowa.  As a result, competition for moisture caused the storms to weaken.  The storms that were severe in Iowa produced high winds in what appears to be several microburst events.  Winds of 74 MPH were recorded at the Ames Airport, with 73 MPH winds measured at a mesonet site in Adair.  A few other reports of severe winds were received with tree damage south of Adair and also in the Earlham area.  There were only a few reports of hail from the storms.  Hail that did occur was limited to an inch or less in diameter.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major late season winter storm affected a portion of northeast Montana beginning late on the evening of the 10th, and continued until about noon on the 12th. The storm produced up to a foot of heavy wet snow, with snow drifts up to 5 feet deep. Low pressure developed in Wyoming on the evening of the 10th and tracked into the Dakotas during the afternoon hours of the 11th. Rain changed to snow late on the evening of the 10th and during the pre dawn hours of the 11th.  Periods of snow continued through the morning of the 12th, and some of the snow fell heavily at times during the day on the 11th. Snowfall ranged from about 3 inches to as much as a foot across most of northeast Montana north of the Missouri River.  Snowdrifts of up to 5 feet were reported in northern Valley County. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The first round of severe thunderstorms to affect southern Illinois occurred during the late morning hours. Most of the severe weather was in the form of large hail during this episode. The first storm became severe just south of Mount Vernon and tracked east along the Hamilton/Wayne County border. Other severe storms developed across the Marion and Herrin areas, producing copious amounts of large hail in Herrin. There was wind damage in Carterville and the Cambria area of Williamson County, where trees and power lines were down. Roads were blocked by fallen trees in Carterville and just south of Cambria. Five to six houses were struck by falling trees, mainly on the west side of Carterville. Major damage occurred to some of the houses. At John A. Logan College near Carterville, numerous trees and limbs were down, destroying fencing and a light pole. These severe storms then moved east and consolidated into a supercell in southern Saline County, just south of Harrisburg. As the supercell crossed Hardin County, a 12-mile long swath of wind damage occurred. The wind damage was primarily in the Shawnee National Forest, resulting in little structural damage until the storm reached Cave-In-Rock, a small town on the Ohio River. At Cave-In-Rock, there were trees down, including at least ten on structures. At the Cave-In-Rock State Park campground near the Ohio River, tents were blown away, and about 20 trees and many more limbs were blown down. Torrential downpours caused street flooding in Cave-In-Rock, and water seeped into the post office and a cafe.

This moist air was being pushed over a warm frontal boundary that lifted northeast across the state.  The airmass became capped over much of the state during the afternoon with a 2.4 degree C. cap in place over southwest Iowa by the early evening.  A small cluster of thunderstorms formed over northwest Iowa during the mid to late afternoon hours.  The storms moved east across the northern tier of Iowa Counties during the late afternoon and evening hours.  They produced hail of three quarters of an inch to an inch in diameter and wind gusts to around 60 MPH.  At one point the storm spiked in intensity.  It produced one and one half inch diameter hail as it passed southwest of Lakota in Kossuth County.

A strong upper level disturbance moved out of Northern Mexico and into to South Texas during the morning of the 6th.  Low level winds ahead of the system backed to the east as winds increased in the mid levels resulting in strong deep layer shear.  Several supercell thunderstorms developed inland over the Coastal Bend.  An HP supercell moved from near Beeville into south-central Goliad county and through northern Refugio, southern Victoria and Calhoun counties.  NWS radar estimated a wide swath of 2-3 inches of rainfall across this area, with localized amounts of 3 to 4 inches, producing flash flooding.  In addition, this storm produced three F0 tornadoes along it's path through Southern Victoria and Calhoun counties.  Additional rotating storms across Kleberg and Nueces county produced flash flooding in Nueces county as well as one confirmed F0 tornado along the coast in Northeast Kleberg county.

A warm, moist, and unstable airmass was in place over Iowa.  The warm front that had produced the convection during the early morning hours of the 8th had become stationary over northern Iowa.  With lifted indices below -10 C. over central Iowa and continued strong moisture advection, thunderstorms erupted over the central and northeast parts of the state during the late afternoon and evening hours.  For the most part, the thunderstorms produced hail during this event.  There were numerous reports of hail of one to two inches in diameter.  Hail reportedly covered the ground in Guthrie County, into parts of Dallas County.  During the later evening hours, the thunderstorms began to sink south and took on a bow echo type configuration, though the line was not a true bow echo.  High winds began to be reported with Cass County being hit the worst.  A swath of damage 7 miles long was reported from west of Lewis to southeast of Lewis.  Embedded in the winds was a small tornado.  The tornado touched down intermittently along the 7 mile path and destroyed or damaged several grain bins and downed numerous trees.  A large corn crib was destroyed southeast of Atlantic and there were numerous reports of trees over highways.  In addition to the hail and high winds, heavy rain occurred from central into parts of west central Iowa.  Flash flooding occurred in Audubon, Guthrie, Madison, and Adair Counties.  Rain fell as the thunderstorms trained and redeveloped repeatedly over the same areas.  Rainfall rates were in the one to three inch per hour range with rainfall total reports of over 4 inches received in a few places in under two hours.  Water flooded over highways, even some U.S. Highways, to as depth of one to two feet.  This resulted in closure of some highways.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several strong to severe thunderstorms developed along the higher terrain of southwest Texas during the late afternoon of the 6th. A cell merger over the northern parts of Big Bend National Park resulted in the development of a severe multicell storm over Persimmon Gap. The National Park Service reported dime to quarter size hail along with strong winds. No wind speed estimates were reported.

An upper level trough remained situated out to the west in Northern Mexico and the Southwest U.S.  A very unstable airmass developed during the afternoon hours across South Texas triggering thunderstorms.  An upper level shortwave rotated out of Mexico during the afternoon providing increasing large-scale ascent, divergence aloft and steepening mid-level lapse rates.  Thunderstorms initially began as supercells across the Rio Grande Plains and Duval and Jim Wells counties during the afternoon and early evening, producing large hail and heavy rain.  The supercells organized into a squall-line during the evening and moved east across the Coastal Bend, producing heavy rainfall and flash flooding.  A wake low formed over the Coastal Bend behind the squall line as it moved into the offshore waters during the late night and early morning hours.  High sustained winds of 40 to 50 mph, with some gusts over 60 mph, developed over the Coastal Bend, Victoria Crossroads region and the bays and nearshore waters. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very unstable airmass was over Iowa and helped kick off the seasons first severe weather outbreak.  At the surface a warm frontal boundary extended nearly east to west across the state and provided the focus for thunderstorm development.  By the late afternoon, lifted indices were approaching -10 C. with CAPE values around 5000 J/kg over western Iowa.  Surface temperatures warmed into the upper 80s with dew points in the low to mid 70s.  A southwest surface wind of 15 to 25 kts pushed over the front.  Northeast of the frontal boundary winds were easterly around 10 to 15 kts.  Actually, the surface boundary was further enhanced by outflow from convective complexes during the day, further sharpening the contrast.  Thunderstorms continued to fire along and north of the boundary through the afternoon and into the evening.  This resulted in widespread flash flooding as very heavy rains fell on areas that had had significant rainfall the previous night.  There were reports in north central into northeast Iowa of 2 to 4 inches of rainfall in a little more than an hours time.  Major flooding took place in the Mason City area where evacuations were taking place.  The thunderstorms became most intense during the afternoon into the early evening.  There were several tornadoes across northeast into north central Iowa.  Most were relatively brief touchdowns and were in open areas.  Reports of multi-vortex tornadoes were received from Grundy County.  The days most significant tornado touched down in Pocahontas County east of Rolfe and tracked into Humboldt County through the Bradgate area.  The tornado damaged or destroyed over 75% of the town of Bradgate (pop 120).  Tornado damage in Bradgate was very extensive impacting most of the town.  Hardly a building was not impacted.   Outbuildings, light structures and garages were heavily damaged or destroyed.  Two homes were destroyed.  Several homes were damaged ranging from minor to extensive. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of heavy rain and snow melt caused poor drainage and creek flooding in the southern part of Berks County. Heavier rain fell from the late morning into the middle of the evening on the 6th. The Manatawny Creek at Spangville was above its 6 foot flood stage from 308 p.m. EST on the 6th through 126 a.m. EST on the 7th. It crested at 6.44 feet at 815 p.m. EST on the 6th. Storm totals included 2.01 inches in Bechtelsville, 1.94 inches in Reading and 1.20 inches in Hamburg.The low pressure system responsible for the heavy rain developed in the western Gulf of Mexico on the 5th. It moved northeast reaching the Tennessee Valley on the evening of the 5th and into the Great Lakes on the morning of the 6th. Its associated warm front moved north from the Carolinas on the morning of the 6th into the lower Delmarva Peninsula during the afternoon of the 6th before stalling. The occluded front associated with the primary low pressure system (It went northeast from the Great Lakes through the Saint Lawrence River Valley) moved through the region during the evening of the 6th and ended the rain. Precipitation initially started as a wintry mix during the late evening of the 5th and changed over to plain rain during the morning of the 6th. Berks County suffered both damage from the icing on trees and wires as well as flooding later during the day.

A slow moving low pressure at both the surface and aloft produced periods of rain across Delaware from the morning of the 12th into the evening of the 13th. The heaviest bursts of rain fell during the afternoon and evening of the 12th and again during the afternoon of the 13th. Two day storm totals averaged around 1.5 inches in New Castle County and 2.75 inches in Kent and Sussex Counties and caused poor drainage flooding and ponding of water in fields. Runoff from the heavy rain caused flooding along the Saint Jones River in Dover on the 14th. Specific storm totals included 3.10 inches in Milford (Kent County), 3.02 inches in Georgetown (Sussex County), 2.67 inches in Dover (Kent County), 2.54 inches in Greenwood and 1.53 inches in Wilmington (New Castle County). The low pressure system responsible for the heavy rain moved from Mississippi the morning of the 12th slowly northeast into Alabama during the evening of the 12th, extreme eastern Tennessee on the morning of the 13th, near Philadelphia early in the evening of the 13th and reached the Berkshires of Massachusetts just after midnight EDT on the 14th. The slow movement permitted this low pressure system to gather moisture from both the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic Ocean and dropped it onto the Middle Atlantic States.

The synoptic situation was very similar to what it was the previous day.  A complex weather situation was in place due to the convection from the previous night.  An outflow boundary extended east to west across northern Missouri.  The synoptic frontal boundary extended from central Nebraska across northern Iowa.  The air was clear over Iowa during the day, allowing for temperatures to recover.  Dew point values also recovered quite rapidly with readings in the upper 60s to low 70s by the late afternoon hours.  Lifted indices dropped into the -5 to -10 C. range by evening with CAPE values approaching 5000 J/kg.  By the evening hours, the frontal boundary and outflow boundary had converged and were located along Interstate 80.  Explosive thunderstorm development took place during the very late afternoon and evening hours in spite of the weak shear profile.  Discrete supercells formed in a narrow line along Interstate 80 from near Des Moines on west.  The storms became tornadic quickly.  To add insult to injury, a strong thunderstorm complex formed over Nebraska and moved east along the line of convection over Iowa.  As the event took shape, all modes of severe weather occurred.  The storms developed so rapidly that there was little more than a half hour from the first hail and wind report to the first tornado touchdown.  Hail and high wind reports were too numerous to mention individually here.  Numerous reports of golf ball size hail were received.  Boone and Story Counties reported some of the largest hail with the event as baseball size hail pelted the are.  There was one report of very large hail northwest of Slater in Story County.  Hail five and one half inches in diameter punched 8 holes through a steel roof.  There was severe house siding and roof damage in the area.  There were numerous tornadoes, especially in the central Iowa Iowa.  At one point there were several supercells around the metropolitan Des Moines area.  Two of the stronger tornadoes touched down west and south of Des Moines.  Fortunately, most of the tornado tracks were over open areas and resulted in little damage.  High winds became a problem, especially after sunset, as the complex from Nebraska moved in.  The system became more of a derecho during the late night hours.  Eighty plus MPH winds pelted southwest Iowa and downed barns and several buildings in Adams and Cass Counties.  A beta bow element formed in central Iowa shortly before midnight.  The bow echo produced a measured wind gust of 106 MPH in northern Warren County.  The high winds continued to push east along Interstate 80 for the next hour or so before it started to weaken. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The morning of May 30 started out with a line of showers and thunderstorms moving into north-central Illinois.  Other thunderstorms developed over portions of east central Illinois and northwest Indiana. The major threat was heavy rain which produced widespread street flooding.  There were also reports of thunderstorm wind damage.  The line of thunderstorms continued to march east through northeast Illinois and northwest Indiana and by early afternoon the line had pushed east of the region.  By mid afternoon a second line of thunderstorms crossed the Mississippi river into western Illinois and other storms developed over east central Illinois and northwest Indiana. The storms continued to move through the area into early evening.   The two lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage.  There were also a few reports of lightning damage associated with these storms.  Flash flooding was a serious problem as a considerable amount of rain had fallen recently in addition to heavy rains associated with these storms.  The storms produced several weak tornadoes over Livingston County Illinois.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and tree limbs were blown down.  Also, trees were down at campground east of Millbrook. Tree limbs were down on a power line in Yorkville.  A tree was down on a car in Little Rock. Another tree was down on a power line 3 miles south of Plano.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Major flooding occurred on the Turkey River as a result of rainfall totals of 8 to 10 inches.  At Garber, a new all-time flood record was established when the river crested at 32.8 feet on May 23.  The previous flood of record occurred on May 17, 1999 when the river crested at 30.91 feet.  At Elkader, the river crested at 25.6 feet on May 23, which threatened to overtop the dike and forced evacuations on the south side of town.  Numerous homes were so badly damaged, residents had to either rebuild or move to a different location.  The town of Elkport (Clayton County) was also hit hard by flooding, with several bridges and highways damaged by high water.  Damage to roads, structures and agricultural land caused by  flood waters was estimated at nearly 3.5 million dollars.
Localized flash flooding was caused by 1 to 2 inches of rain in less than two hours.

Rainfall totals of 6 to 8 inches caused the Cedar River to flood.  The river crested at 16.5 feet on May 23 in Charles City, which forced the evacuation of some residents and closure of roads.  In addition, several farm fields near the river were flooded, damaging newly planted crops of corn and soybeans.

A strong upper level disturbance moved out of Northern Mexico and into to South Texas during the morning of the 6th.  Low level winds ahead of the system backed to the east as winds increased in the mid levels resulting in strong deep layer shear.  Several supercell thunderstorms developed inland over the Coastal Bend.  An HP supercell moved from near Beeville into south-central Goliad county and through northern Refugio, southern Victoria and Calhoun counties.  NWS radar estimated a wide swath of 2-3 inches of rainfall across this area, with localized amounts of 3 to 4 inches, producing flash flooding.  In addition, this storm produced three F0 tornadoes along it's path through Southern Victoria and Calhoun counties.  Additional rotating storms across Kleberg and Nueces county produced flash flooding in Nueces county as well as one confirmed F0 tornado along the coast in Northeast Kleberg county.

Several severe thunderstorms affected the northeast Permian Basin of west Texas during the late afternoon and evening of the 25th. These storms developed near a dryline/cold front triple point. A second supercell tracked east, then southeast across northern Mitchell County. This storm produced two tornadoes, baseball size hail, and damaging winds in the vicinity of Colorado City and Loraine.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful spring storm brought heavy wet snow to many higher elevations areas of southern Colorado.  Generous amounts of 10 to 20 inches were common in the highest elevations.  Some of the higher snow amounts in populated areas were:  6 inches at Rye in Pueblo county...7 inches and more at Leadville in Lake county...12 inches at Walsenburg in Huerfano county and Westcliffe in Custer county...14 inches at Cuchara in Huerfano county and Rosita in Custer county...15 inches 10 miles northwest of Salida in Chaffee county...18 inches 8 miles west of Westcliffe...and 19 inches in La Veta in Huerfano county.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: An eastward moving thundertsorm complex in the southeastern Gulf of Mexico collapsed as it moved north of the Florida Keys. The cold outflow left over from the storm created wind gusts of 40 to 50 knots along the coastal areas of southwest Florida. Winds at the Fort Myers Southwest Florida Regional Airport were sustained from 30 to 36 knots with the peak gust of 50 knots occurring at 3:17 AM EST.   A 737 plane was pushed into a jetway bridge and damaged both the wing and the bridge.  Emergency Management said the winds mostly uprooted trees and downed power lines.  Cape Coral city officials estimated $63,450 in damage to roofs, carports, lanais, and other structures. The winds ripped the metal roof off an airplane hangar at the Pine Island Airport near Bokeella.  Utility officials said Tuesday's winds left about 27,000 Lee County residents without power.  Minor beach erosion occurred at Fort Myers Beach, Lovers Key State Park, and Bonita Beach. The gusty winds reached as far north as the Sunshine Skyway Bridge in the Tampa Bay area where where sustained winds of around 30 knots with gusts to 38 knots were reported between 3:52 AM EST to about 5:15 AM EST.  No significant damage was reported north of Lee County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist, and unstable airmass was in place over Iowa.  The warm front that had produced the convection during the early morning hours of the 8th had become stationary over northern Iowa.  With lifted indices below -10 C. over central Iowa and continued strong moisture advection, thunderstorms erupted over the central and northeast parts of the state during the late afternoon and evening hours.  For the most part, the thunderstorms produced hail during this event.  There were numerous reports of hail of one to two inches in diameter.  Hail reportedly covered the ground in Guthrie County, into parts of Dallas County.  During the later evening hours, the thunderstorms began to sink south and took on a bow echo type configuration, though the line was not a true bow echo.  High winds began to be reported with Cass County being hit the worst.  A swath of damage 7 miles long was reported from west of Lewis to southeast of Lewis.  Embedded in the winds was a small tornado.  The tornado touched down intermittently along the 7 mile path and destroyed or damaged several grain bins and downed numerous trees.  A large corn crib was destroyed southeast of Atlantic and there were numerous reports of trees over highways.  In addition to the hail and high winds, heavy rain occurred from central into parts of west central Iowa.  Flash flooding occurred in Audubon, Guthrie, Madison, and Adair Counties.  Rain fell as the thunderstorms trained and redeveloped repeatedly over the same areas.  Rainfall rates were in the one to three inch per hour range with rainfall total reports of over 4 inches received in a few places in under two hours.  Water flooded over highways, even some U.S. Highways, to as depth of one to two feet.  This resulted in closure of some highways.

Hail up to the size of baseballs was observed along with many areas reporting hail on the ground ranging from 3 inches deep to 2 feet deep. The hail damaged numerous structures and vehicles with several people also needing their vehicles towed or dug out of the hail on streets across the city. Damage estimates across the Oklahoma City metro were 100 million dollars. Storms also produced two tornadoes in Ellis county in northwest Oklahoma with no known damage reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough remained situated out to the west in Northern Mexico and the Southwest U.S.  A very unstable airmass developed during the afternoon hours across South Texas triggering thunderstorms.  An upper level shortwave rotated out of Mexico during the afternoon providing increasing large-scale ascent, divergence aloft and steepening mid-level lapse rates.  Thunderstorms initially began as supercells across the Rio Grande Plains and Duval and Jim Wells counties during the afternoon and early evening, producing large hail and heavy rain.  The supercells organized into a squall-line during the evening and moved east across the Coastal Bend, producing heavy rainfall and flash flooding.  A wake low formed over the Coastal Bend behind the squall line as it moved into the offshore waters during the late night and early morning hours.  High sustained winds of 40 to 50 mph, with some gusts over 60 mph, developed over the Coastal Bend, Victoria Crossroads region and the bays and nearshore waters.  Damage associated with these winds was mainly confined to tree limbs, however a tug boat in Port Oconnor was reportedly damaged. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm moving southeast from the Gulf of Alaska, picked up tropical moisture before it moved onshore. The warmer air mass caused the snow level to remain high during most of the precipitaion event, so that measured snow fall was less than eight inches in the mountains. However strong winds did occur in the mountains and heavy rain fell over much of Southern California. Most roads along the foothills of the San Bernardino Mountains, both on the north and south side were closed due to flooding and mud slides. Also, over Orange County and San Diego County, several major highways and secondary roads were closed due to flooding.

The combination of heavy rain and snow melt caused poor drainage flooding in Kent and Sussex Counties. Heavier rain fell from the middle of the morning into the middle of the evening on the 6th. Strong gradient winds affected south-central and southeast Wisconsin for many hours.  Maximum wind  gusts were generally in the 40 to 49 kt range (46 to 57 mph).  There were numerous newspaper reports of broken tree branches hitting power lines with a resultant power outage.  Strong cross winds may have been indirectly responsible for the death of a motorcyclist who lost control and crashed in a farm field in the Town of Yorkville of Racine County.  In Sheboygan County near Glenbeulah the strong winds moved a silo off its foundation about 16 inches, ripped a door off a barn, and knocked down some large trees.  In the city of Sheboygan the strong winds blew in several windows at a car dealership.  Near the city of Oregon (Dane Co.) a home was damaged by a large, wind-toppled tree.  Electrical companies estimated that about 20,000 customers in south-central and southeast Wisconsin lost power at one time or another.

A quick moving occluded front and a low pressure system that developed on it off the Delmarva Peninsula dropped a quick one to four inches across the northern half of New Jersey during the first half of the day on the 8th. Some locally higher accumulations occurred in Morris and Sussex Counties. Most of the accumulations were on grassy surfaces except for extreme northwest New Jersey where some slushy snow accumulated on secondary and tertiary roads. Precipitation began as rain around midnight EST on the 8th. As the low pressure system intensified off the Delmarva Peninsula and precipitation fell heavier, the rain changed to snow in most areas between 3 a.m. and 5 a.m. EST. When the precipitation intensity weakened at the end of the event, in some places the snow changed back to rain before ending by noon EST. Specific accumulations included 4.5 inches in Highland Lakes (Sussex County), 4.3 inches in Barry Lakes (Sussex County), 4.0 inches in Milton (Morris County), 3.6 inches in Marcella (Morris County), 3.3 inches in Budd Lake (Morris County) and Clarksburg (Monmouth County), 2.0 inches in Chatham (Morris County), Blairstown (Warren County) and Flemington (Hunterdon County), 1.7 inches in Hightstown (Mercer County), 1.6 inches in South River (Middlesex County), 1.5 inches in Wertsville (Hunterdon County), 1.3 inches in New Brunswick (Middlesex County) and 1.2 inches in Pottersville and Belle Mead (Somerset County).An occluded front moved from the Upper Mississippi Valley on the evening of the 6th, to the Great Lakes the morning of the 7th, to central Pennsylvania the evening of the 7th. A new low pressure system formed on the triple point of this occluded front over the Delmarva coastal waters during the early morning of the 8th. It intensified rapidly, but was also moving offshore quickly. Before it moved far enough offshore, it gave the northern half of New Jersey several hours of accumulating snow.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A bridge along Interstate 20 just east-northeast of Toyah over the normally dry Salt Draw failed Sunday evening. This failure was the result of fast-moving flood waters originating from previous heavy rainfall over the Davis Mountains. Hydrologists also credited a residual flow of water through the draw from the Toyah dike break early Sunday for contributing to the gradual process that caused the bridge to collapse. Authorities said that advance warning of additional runoff and flooding allowed the interstate to be closed to both eastbound and westbound traffic at the first sign of danger to the bridge. A state official for the Texas Department of Transportation said that 86 feet of roadway in the eastbound lanes fell into the river, and that additional 40-foot segments on each side of the river were also damaged. On the westbound side, one of the upright supports holding the bridge had moved six to eight inches, opening a crack in the roadway.  No fatalities were reported with the bridge collapse, however, five indirect fatalities occurred in a multi-vehicle collision along a detour, U.S. Highway 285, south of Pecos.
House windows and cars were heavily damaged.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A series of thunderstorms, that began on Saturday April 3rd and continued into the early afternoon on Sunday, resulted in significant flooding over Lea County, especially over the eastern portions of the county.  Many roads across the eastern half of Lea County were closed due to flooding including State Routes 8, 18, 176, and U.S. Highway 62/180.  During Sunday morning, the community of Nadine, between Eunice and Hobbs, also reported significant flooding.

During the evening of April 3rd, a National Weather Service spotter reported Dark Canyon Road, five miles east of State Highway 137, was under seven feet of water.  Additional flooding over southwestern portions of Carlsbad was reported by local law enforcement and the public.  Just after midnight, early Sunday morning,  U.S. Highway 285 became impassable due to flooding ten miles northwest of Carlsbad.  Flooding along County Roads 658 and 672 southwest of Carlsbad resulted in several evacuations and helicopter rescues during the early morning hours on Sunday along Dark Canyon Draw.  As late as Sunday afternoon, flooding of low-lying areas around Carlsbad continued along the Pecos River, as well as along Dark Canyon, Dagger, Rocky Arroyo, and Hackberry Draws.An Eddy County flood survey revealed that three different factors contributed to the record flooding in and near Carlsbad. Flood waters from Rocky Arroyo Draw fed into the Pecos River north of Avalon Reservoir. This flow along with heavy rainfall from thunderstorms resulted in a required release of water from the Avalon Reservoir. Radar estimated rainfall totals of three to four inches near and west of Avalon Reservoir between 900 PM MST on April 3rd through 100 AM MST on Sunday, April 4th. Releases from the reservoir began near 800 PM MST on April 3rd, with a measured peak rate of 14,800 cfs (cubic-feet per second) at around 400 AM MDT Sunday morning. This release of water eliminated the potential danger of a dam failure, but resulted in the washout of Callaway Drive just downstream from the release point on Avalon Reservoir. The second factor contributing to the record flooding was extremely high flow through the Dark Canyon Draw into downtown Carlsbad. Radar estimated rainfall totals of one to three inches over and southwest of Dark Canyon Draw during the evening and overnight hours of Saturday April 3rd. This rainfall led to catastrophic flash flooding along the Dark Canyon Draw from southwest portions of Carlsbad into the downtown area. A wall of water moved down Dark Canyon Draw at approximately 130 AM MST Sunday morning. The third factor that contributed to the flooding was the failure at several points of the Carlsbad Irrigation District (CID) canals. These CID channels, used primarily to irrigate area alfalfa fields, began failing due to runoff crossing perpendicular to the CID channels. This runoff was due to 8-12 inches of rainfall in the previous three days. Erosion of the channels began occurring due to the high volume of water flowing over them. As the channels finally failed, water flowed into adjacent neighborhoods. The community hardest hit by this runoff was the La Huerta neighborhood in northeastern Carlsbad.  As a result of this flooding, 6 to 12 inches of water was left standing throughout most of the La Huerta area with higher amounts at isolated points.
Golfball to baseball size hail fell in Balmorhea and also along Farm to Market Road 1450 east of Pecos.Hail was still covering FM 1450 at 915 pm that evening.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The cold front that had moved southeast across the state the previous night became stationary across southern Iowa by the morning of the 17th.  A sharp contrast in dew point temperatures was found across the front.  Dew points were in the upper 50s to mid 60s south of the front, with dew points in the 30s north of it.  During the late afternoon the front began to return north as a warm front.  By evening a strengthening southerly jet in the low levels impinged on the front with wind speeds around 50 kts.  The overall low levels of the atmosphere were relatively dry and the airmass was capped initially.  The LCL height was around 750 mb.  There atmosphere was quite unstable with Lifted Indices in the -6 to -10 C range.  CAPE values were in the 2500 to 3500 J/kg range.  Thunderstorms erupted over northern Iowa shortly after sunset.  The storms formed into discrete supercells.  A tornado touched down east of Mason City from one of the stronger cells.  It was in open area and did not cause any damage during its brief touchdown.  The dominant severe weather mode for the event was hail.  Baseball size hail fell in Palo Alto County in Mallard.  There were numerous reports of hail three quarters of an inch to one and one quarter of an inch in diameter.  The largest hail was around two inches in diameter in Palo Alto County.  Hail reportedly covered the ground as the storms passed.  During the late stages of the event, a thunderstorms produced high winds as it swept across Interstate 35 west of Northwood in Worth County.  Two vehicles and one semi-tractortrailer truck were blown off of the interstate near mile post 214.  In addition, one telephone was blown down by the high wind.

The synoptic situation was very similar to what it was the previous day.  A complex weather situation was in place due to the convection from the previous night.  An outflow boundary extended east to west across northern Missouri.  The synoptic frontal boundary extended from central Nebraska across northern Iowa.  The air was clear over Iowa during the day, allowing for temperatures to recover.  Dew point values also recovered quite rapidly with readings in the upper 60s to low 70s by the late afternoon hours.  Lifted indices dropped into the -5 to -10 C. range by evening with CAPE values approaching 5000 J/kg.  By the evening hours, the frontal boundary and outflow boundary had converged and were located along Interstate 80.  Explosive thunderstorm development took place during the very late afternoon and evening hours in spite of the weak shear profile.  Discrete supercells formed in a narrow line along Interstate 80 from near Des Moines on west.  The storms became tornadic quickly.  To add insult to injury, a strong thunderstorm complex formed over Nebraska and moved east along the line of convection over Iowa.  As the event took shape, all modes of severe weather occurred.  The storms developed so rapidly that there was little more than a half hour from the first hail and wind report to the first tornado touchdown.  Hail and high wind reports were too numerous to mention individually here.  Numerous reports of golf ball size hail were received.  Boone and Story Counties reported some of the largest hail with the event as baseball size hail pelted the are.  There was one report of very large hail northwest of Slater in Story County.  Hail five and one half inches in diameter punched 8 holes through a steel roof.  There was severe house siding and roof damage in the area.  There were numerous tornadoes, especially in the central Iowa Iowa.  At one point there were several supercells around the metropolitan Des Moines area.  Two of the stronger tornadoes touched down west and south of Des Moines.  Fortunately, most of the tornado tracks were over open areas and resulted in little damage.  High winds became a problem, especially after sunset, as the complex from Nebraska moved in.  The system became more of a derecho during the late night hours.  Eighty plus MPH winds pelted southwest Iowa and downed barns and several buildings in Adams and Cass Counties.  A beta bow element formed in central Iowa shortly before midnight.  The bow echo produced a measured wind gust of 106 MPH in northern Warren County.  The high winds continued to push east along Interstate 80 for the next hour or so before it started to weaken.  The other major problem was with heavy rain.  The convection from the previous night set the stage by saturating soils.  The echos trained for several hours across central Iowa with very heavy rainfall.  Rainfall rates of 4 to 5 inches per hour were common under the heavier cells.  Several locations received 2 to 5 inch rainfalls in under  two hours, resulting in widespread flash flooding.  Reports of major highways being inundated by water were common.  By the end of the night, a swath of 4 to 9 inch rainfall was evident north of Interstate 80.  Longer term river flooding became a major problem by the morning of the 23rd.  There were two lightning related injuries.  Two people were injured when they were struck by lightning out of doors in Nevada.  The lightning struck close by as they were carrying groceries into their home.  The jolt caused them to fall, resulting in laceration to the head.

To add insult to injury, a strong thunderstorm complex formed over Nebraska and moved east along the line of convection over Iowa.  As the event took shape, all modes of severe weather occurred.  The storms developed so rapidly that there was little more than a half hour from the first hail and wind report to the first tornado touchdown.  Hail and high wind reports were too numerous to mention individually here.  Numerous reports of golf ball size hail were received.  Boone and Story Counties reported some of the largest hail with the event as baseball size hail pelted the are.  There was one report of very large hail northwest of Slater in Story County.  Hail five and one half inches in diameter punched 8 holes through a steel roof.  There was severe house siding and roof damage in the area.  There were numerous tornadoes, especially in the central Iowa Iowa.  At one point there were several supercells around the metropolitan Des Moines area.  Two of the stronger tornadoes touched down west and south of Des Moines.  Fortunately, most of the tornado tracks were over open areas and resulted in little damage.  High winds became a problem, especially after sunset, as the complex from Nebraska moved in.  The system became more of a derecho during the late night hours.  Eighty plus MPH winds pelted southwest Iowa and downed barns and several buildings in Adams and Cass Counties.  A beta bow element formed in central Iowa shortly before midnight.  The bow echo produced a measured wind gust of 106 MPH in northern Warren County.  The high winds continued to push east along Interstate 80 for the next hour or so before it started to weaken.  The other major problem was with heavy rain.  The convection from the previous night set the stage by saturating soils.  The echos trained for several hours across central Iowa with very heavy rainfall.  Rainfall rates of 4 to 5 inches per hour were common under the heavier cells.  Several locations received 2 to 5 inch rainfalls in under  two hours, resulting in widespread flash flooding.  Reports of major highways being inundated by water were common.  By the end of the night, a swath of 4 to 9 inch rainfall was evident north of Interstate 80.  Longer term river flooding became a major problem by the morning of the 23rd.  There were two lightning related injuries.  Two people were injured when they were struck by lightning out of doors in Nevada.  The lightning struck close by as they were carrying groceries into their home.  The jolt caused them to fall, resulting in laceration to the head.

The morning of May 30 started out with a line of showers and thunderstorms moving into north-central Illinois.  Other thunderstorms developed over portions of east central Illinois and northwest Indiana. The major threat was heavy rain which produced widespread street flooding.  There were also reports of thunderstorm wind damage.  The line of thunderstorms continued to march east through northeast Illinois and northwest Indiana and by early afternoon the line had pushed east of the region.  By mid afternoon a second line of thunderstorms crossed the Mississippi river into western Illinois and other storms developed over east central Illinois and northwest Indiana. The storms continued to move through the area into early evening.   The two lines of thunderstorms produced widespread tree damage.  There were also a few reports of lightning damage associated with these storms.  Flash flooding was a serious problem as a considerable amount of rain had fallen recently in addition to heavy rains associated with these storms.  The storms produced several weak tornadoes over Livingston County Illinois.

A cold front moved southeast slowly southeast across Iowa during the day on the 17th.  The surface front moved about half way through the state, while the front at 850 mb remained over the northwest part of the state.  The airmass was unstable, but not extremely unstable.  Lifted indices were around -2 to -5 C during the afternoon.  The convective inhibition had dropped to zero by mid afternoon with CAPE values around 1500 J/kg.  Thunderstorms erupted in the vicinity to just north of the surface cold front by late afternoon.  An MCS developed over southwest Iowa and tracked east across the state during the late afternoon and evening.  The main severe weather mode from this system was hail.  There were numerous reports of three quarter to one inch diameter hail during the period.  Some of the larger hail reached golf ball to baseball in size.  The largest hail fell in Madison County in the Winterset area as baseball size hail pummeled the area twice.  A few storms produced high winds.  One of the stronger storms was over Adams County.  In what appeared to be a macroburst, winds of around 60 MPH downed power poles and  a few outbuildings east of the Corning area.  The power poles were set on fire as they fell.  Later in the evening, over Monroe and Mahaska Counties, a thunderstorm turned into a bow echo segment and caused considerable damage near the Eddyville area.  One mile east of Eddyville on 340th St. along the Wapello-Mahaska county line was the hardest hit area.  Two farmstead received extensive damage around 9:15 p.m.  A microburst likely occurred on the farmstead located along the north side of the road (western-most farmstead), followed by a damage path spreading one-quarter mile east-southeast to a farmstead along the south side of the road.  At the southern farmstead, two farm outbuildings were destroyed.  Three poles rooted five feet into the ground were lifted complete out of the ground.  The roof of a shed was peeled back.   Pieces of the outbuildings from the northern farmstead spread out to the east and southeast up to 150 yards in width near the southern farmstead.  Length of the visible damage path was around ½ mile.  Persons in both farmsteads reported the duration of the strongest winds to be from 20 to 30 seconds.  Maximum winds were estimated to be around 85 mph.  When all was said and done, high winds flattened a barn and several outbuildings, silos, and trees.  Boards from the barn were driven through a car east of Eddyville along the southern Mahaska County border.  Several roads were blocked by fallen trees throughout the area.  Several hogs were killed when one of the barns collapsed near Eddyville.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another round of severe thunderstorms affected southern Illinois during the afternoon and evening hours, following the late morning round of storms. This round began with a swath of large hail near the western Perry/Jackson County line. Numerous trees were blown down near Galatia. The final severe storm of this episode was a long-lived storm cluster that tracked east from the Mount Vernon area to the Wabash River. This storm produced golf-ball hail west of Mount Vernon, then downed trees and power lines in Crossville in White County. A mobile home was unroofed one mile southeast of Crossville, and its contents were damaged by rain. Otherwise, most of the events during this episode were isolated dime to nickel size hail.

An intense low pressure moved across the northern tier of states during the day on the 27th.  Very strong south-southwest winds developed with profilers indicating wind of 50 to 65 kts within the lowest range gates.  Temperatures warmed into the mid 80s to low 90s with the atmosphere becoming adiabatic to between 750 and 600 mb, allowing for strong mixing down to the surface.  Winds increased during the day and reached high wind criteria by the early afternoon.  Most of the state saw sustained winds of 40 MPH or higher.  Several locations gusting to between 60 and 65 MPH.  The winds also produced blowing dust around the state.  Isolated reports of visibility reduced to near zero were received.  Spotty damage occurred around the state.  An 18 inch tree limb broke off and fell through the roof of a house in Windsor Heights.  A two to three foot diameter tree was snapped off at the base in Ames.  There were numerous reports of power outages caused by downed tree limbs.  In Union County, a 200 X 40 foot chicken house had the roof blown off.  There were several head of cattle in addition to the chickens contained therein trapped in the debris.

A major hail storm moved through the Oklahoma City metro on this day primarily affecting the western and northern sides of the city. Hail up to the size of baseballs was observed along with many areas reporting hail on the ground ranging from 3 inches deep to 2 feet deep. The hail damaged numerous structures and vehicles with several people also needing their vehicles towed or dug out of the hail on streets across the city. Damage estimates across the Oklahoma City metro were 100 million dollars. Storms also produced two tornadoes in Ellis county in northwest Oklahoma with no known damage reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Once again it was a very active severe weather day over Iowa.  The frontal system that had moved through the state on the night of the 22nd was returning north as a warm front.  This time Iowa did not get completely into the warm sector.  The surface front was dragged north into Iowa by low pressure that moved out of Kansas northeast into central Iowa by the mid to late evening.  The airmass was pushed southeast out of the state by a cold front that passed through the state during the evening and early morning hours.  The airmass in the warm sector became very unstable.  Lifted indices were around -13 C with CAPE values greater than 5000 J/kg by the late afternoon.  The air advected north into Iowa during the day and into the evening.  Thunderstorms erupted in two places.  The first to affect the DSM CWA was the development of several elevated supercells over west central into southwest Iowa.  The storms continued to lift east and northeast across the area.  A few tornadoes touched down, however with the very elevated nature of the storms it was very difficult for the tornadoes to reach the ground.  By the late afternoon, a solid squall line developed along the cold front.  The line took on a Line Echo Wave Pattern by evening.  Several segments of the line bowed out, resulting in high winds.  At times the winds reached 80 MPH.  One of the thunderstorms produced high winds in the Early area of Sac County.  They overturned a semi-tractortrailer truck, causing $80,000 damage and causing minor injuries to the driver.  Tornadoes that formed along this line actually formed where the Rear Flank Downdraft cut through the line.  A clear meso was formed and the small tornadoes advanced around the meso and were in front of the thunderstorm line.  Touchdowns were all brief.  Hail was common with the stronger storm, with much of it in the one to one and three-quarter inch in diameter.  Given the antecedent soil conditions in Iowa, flash flooding became a major issue.  Numerous counties reported flash flooding as rainfall of one to 4 inches in spots resulted in flooded highways.  The thunderstorms formed into an MCC by the early evening hours.  As they moved out of the state, they delivered one more punch to the state.  High winds developed in the wake of the complex.  Several counties of north central, northeast, and central Iowa received high winds.  Damage occurred in several locations to both trees and out buildings.  Sustained winds across the area were in the 25 to 45 MPH range with some higher gusts.  Clarion reported a wind gust of 63 MPH for the highest wind gust reported.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A strong late season winter storm moved through the Ohio Valley, producing a wide swath of three or more inches across much of west central and central Ohio. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A narrow swath of heavy wet snow hammered a small section of the south central Nebraska during the early morning hours of April 12th.  The band of snow, which was anywhere from 5 to 8 inches, fell along a 30 mile wide line from south of Cambridge in Furnas county to near Red Cloud in Webster county. Specifically, Beaver City reported 7.5 inches of snow, Riverton 7.0 inches and Franklin, Wilsonville and Cambridge all had 6 inches of white stuff. The snow did bring some beneficial moisture of one-third to one-half inch to this drought stricken area.

Significant damage occurred on the south side of Dubuque, Iowa with numerous trees and power lines down and a radio tower mangled. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: 3 low-topped supercell thunderstorms dropped down at least 1 tornado a piece and a total of 6 tornadoes across Central Indiana during the late afternoon and early evening of April 20. All of the tornadoes were F0 or F1 in rating. The worst damage occurred in Kokomo as 3 homes were damaged and a skating rink and trucking company had significant damage totaling around 3 million dollars. There were also 1 minor injury. The town of Jamestown along the Hendricks/Boone county border also was hit hard with significant damage to a dozen homes totaling 1.65 million dollars.  There were also 8 minor injuries, 1 as a result of his semi being overturned along Interstate 74.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado associated with a low-topped supercell touched down a quarter of a mile south of the Boone/Hendricks county line in Hendricks county. The tornado continued northeast through Jamestown and into Boone county causing significant damage to a dozen homes. 2 homes had their roofs blown completely off and tossed several hundred feet into a corn field. There were 8 minor injuries including one man whose semi was blown over along Interstate 74. Estimated wind speeds were around 110 mph or on the high end of an F1 rating.

A slow moving low pressure at both the surface and aloft produced periods of rain across New Jersey from the morning of the 12th into the evening of the 13th. The heaviest bursts of rain fell during the evening of the 12th, before sunrise on the 13th, around Noon EDT on the 13th and during the evening of the 13th. The rain was heavy enough to cause flooding along sections of the North Branch of the Raritan River and the Millstone River. The Griggstown Causeway was closed because of flooding along the Millstone River. The Millstone River at Griggstown was above its 10 foot flood stage from 9 a.m. EDT on the 13th through 515 a.m. EDT on the 15th. It crested at 15.1 feet at 515 a.m. EDT on the 14th. The North Branch of the Raritan River at South Branch was above its 6.9 foot flood stage from 1118 p.m. EDT on the 13th through 419 a.m. EDT on the 14th. It crested at 145 a.m. EDT on the 14th. Specific storm totals included 2.40 inches in Bound Brook, 2.37 inches in Somerville, 1.77 inches in Pottersville and 1.70 inches in North Plainfield. The low pressure system responsible for the flooding moved from Mississippi the morning of the 12th slowly northeast into Alabama during the evening of the 12th, extreme eastern Tennessee on the morning of the 13th, near Philadelphia early in the evening of the 13th and reached the Berkshires of Massachusetts just after midnight EDT on the 14th. The slow movement permitted this low pressure system to gather moisture from both the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic Ocean and dropped it onto the Middle Atlantic States.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The cold front that had moved southeast across the state the previous night became stationary across southern Iowa by the morning of the 17th.  A sharp contrast in dew point temperatures was found across the front.  Dew points were in the upper 50s to mid 60s south of the front, with dew points in the 30s north of it.  During the late afternoon the front began to return north as a warm front.  By evening a strengthening southerly jet in the low levels impinged on the front with wind speeds around 50 kts.  The overall low levels of the atmosphere were relatively dry and the airmass was capped initially.  The LCL height was around 750 mb.  There atmosphere was quite unstable with Lifted Indices in the -6 to -10 C range.  CAPE values were in the 2500 to 3500 J/kg range.  Thunderstorms erupted over northern Iowa shortly after sunset.  The storms formed into discrete supercells.  A tornado touched down east of Mason City from one of the stronger cells.  It was in open area and did not cause any damage during its brief touchdown.  The dominant severe weather mode for the event was hail.  Baseball size hail fell in Palo Alto County in Mallard.  There were numerous reports of hail three quarters of an inch to one and one quarter of an inch in diameter.  The largest hail was around two inches in diameter in Palo Alto County.  Hail reportedly covered the ground as the storms passed.  During the late stages of the event, a thunderstorms produced high winds as it swept across Interstate 35 west of Northwood in Worth County.  Two vehicles and one semi-tractortrailer truck were blown off of the interstate near mile post 214.  In addition, one telephone was blown down by the high wind.

Minor to moderate flooding impacted the Connecticut River, as a result of 2 to 4 inches of rain over a three day period, combined with upstream snowmelt in northern New England.  Flooding affected many low lying areas and forced the closure of more susceptible roadways.  No estimate of flood damage was available.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Connecticut River at Middletown
