The warm front that had produced the convection during the early morning hours of the 8th had become stationary over northern Iowa.  With lifted indices below -10 C. over central Iowa and continued strong moisture advection, thunderstorms erupted over the central and northeast parts of the state during the late afternoon and evening hours.  For the most part, the thunderstorms produced hail during this event.  There were numerous reports of hail of one to two inches in diameter.  Hail reportedly covered the ground in Guthrie County, into parts of Dallas County.  During the later evening hours, the thunderstorms began to sink south and took on a bow echo type configuration, though the line was not a true bow echo.  High winds began to be reported with Cass County being hit the worst.  A swath of damage 7 miles long was reported from west of Lewis to southeast of Lewis.  Embedded in the winds was a small tornado.  The tornado touched down intermittently along the 7 mile path and destroyed or damaged several grain bins and downed numerous trees.  A large corn crib was destroyed southeast of Atlantic and there were numerous reports of trees over highways.  In addition to the hail and high winds, heavy rain occurred from central into parts of west central Iowa.  Flash flooding occurred in Audubon, Guthrie, Madison, and Adair Counties.  Rain fell as the thunderstorms trained and redeveloped repeatedly over the same areas.  Rainfall rates were in the one to three inch per hour range with rainfall total reports of over 4 inches received in a few places in under two hours.  Water flooded over highways, even some U.S. Highways, to as depth of one to two feet.  This resulted in closure of some highways.

An intense low pressure moved across the northern tier of states during the day on the 27th.  Very strong south-southwest winds developed with profilers indicating wind of 50 to 65 kts within the lowest range gates.  Temperatures warmed into the mid 80s to low 90s with the atmosphere becoming adiabatic to between 750 and 600 mb, allowing for strong mixing down to the surface.  Winds increased during the day and reached high wind criteria by the early afternoon.  Most of the state saw sustained winds of 40 MPH or higher.  Several locations gusting to between 60 and 65 MPH.  The winds also produced blowing dust around the state.  Isolated reports of visibility reduced to near zero were received.  Spotty damage occurred around the state.  An 18 inch tree limb broke off and fell through the roof of a house in Windsor Heights.  A two to three foot diameter tree was snapped off at the base in Ames.  There were numerous reports of power outages caused by downed tree limbs.  In Union County, a 200 X 40 foot chicken house had the roof blown off.  There were several head of cattle in addition to the chickens contained therein trapped in the debris.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A line of strong thunderstorms had stuck Crystal City near 1240 pm CST.  Although individual storms were moving toward the northeast, the line appeared to be moving to the southeast.  The downburst winds were all discharged toward the southwest, as all damage around Crystal City area was blown in that direction.  Damage was severe in Crystal City.  Leaves had been shredded from trees and plastered onto the sides of the cars and houses, and streets were covered with the shredded leaves.  Homes had damage to their outside walls, roofs, and windows.  What was shocking was to see the piles of semi-melted hail still as high as 2 feet in some of the drifts created by the flooding.  In spite of the fact that the hail had been melting for over 24 hours when the survey was made, it was still piled in spotty waves across the city from east to west and north to south.  Hail was reported to have been as large as 1.5 to 2 inches in diameter, with a couple of reports of hail to 3 inches.  The high winds, combined with hail and rain, caused widespread damage to homes, destroying two mobile homes and the roofs of two houses.  Several dozen homes in Crystal City sustained some type of damage.  Some of the worst damage occurred at the library and the H.E.B. grocery store.  The metal roof was blown off the library and deposited on the southwest side of the building.  The roof of the H.E.B. grocery store collapsed. A slow moving low pressure at both the surface and aloft produced periods of rain across Eastern Pennsylvania from the morning of the 12th into the evening of the 13th. The heaviest bursts of rain fell during the afternoon and evening of the 12th and again around Noon EDT and the early evening of the 13th. Thunderstorms exacerbated the heavy rain during the early evening of the 13th. In the one hour period ending at 844 p.m. EDT on the 13th, 0.73 inches of rain fell at the Philadelphia International Airport. This heavy rain led to flooding along the Pennypack Creek within the city. Two day storm totals averaged around 2.5 inches and caused poor drainage flooding and ponding of water during heavier precipitation bursts. Precipitation amounts were lighter elsewhere across Eastern Pennsylvania. Specific storm totals included 3.12 inches in Neshaminy Falls (Bucks County), 3.02 inches at the Northeast Philadelphia Airport, 2.63 inches in Southampton (Bucks County), 2.20 inches at the Franklin Institute within Philadelphia, 2.19 inches at the Philadelphia International Airport, 2.01 inches in Sellersville (Bucks County), 1.80 inches in Springfield Township (Delaware County) and Doylestown (Bucks County), 1.78 inches in Perkasie (Bucks County), 1.70 inches in Fricks (Bucks County), 1.61 inches in West Chester (Chester County) and 1.45 inches in Pottstown (Montgomery County). The low pressure system responsible for the heavy rain moved from Mississippi the morning of the 12th slowly northeast into Alabama during the evening of the 12th, extreme eastern Tennessee on the morning of the 13th, near Philadelphia early in the evening of the 13th and reached the Berkshires of Massachusetts just after midnight EDT on the 14th. The slow movement permitted this low pressure system to gather moisture from both the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic Ocean and dropped it onto the Middle Atlantic States.

A warm, moist, and unstable airmass was in place over Iowa.  The warm front that had produced the convection during the early morning hours of the 8th had become stationary over northern Iowa.  With lifted indices below -10 C. over central Iowa and continued strong moisture advection, thunderstorms erupted over the central and northeast parts of the state during the late afternoon and evening hours.  For the most part, the thunderstorms produced hail during this event.  There were numerous reports of hail of one to two inches in diameter.  Hail reportedly covered the ground in Guthrie County, into parts of Dallas County.  During the later evening hours, the thunderstorms began to sink south and took on a bow echo type configuration, though the line was not a true bow echo.  High winds began to be reported with Cass County being hit the worst.  A swath of damage 7 miles long was reported from west of Lewis to southeast of Lewis.  Embedded in the winds was a small tornado.  The tornado touched down intermittently along the 7 mile path and destroyed or damaged several grain bins and downed numerous trees.  A large corn crib was destroyed southeast of Atlantic and there were numerous reports of trees over highways.  In addition to the hail and high winds, heavy rain occurred from central into parts of west central Iowa.  Flash flooding occurred in Audubon, Guthrie, Madison, and Adair Counties.  Rain fell as the thunderstorms trained and redeveloped repeatedly over the same areas.  Rainfall rates were in the one to three inch per hour range with rainfall total reports of over 4 inches received in a few places in under two hours.  Water flooded over highways, even some U.S. Highways, to as depth of one to two feet.  This resulted in closure of some highways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level trough remained situated out to the west in Northern Mexico and the Southwest U.S.  A very unstable airmass developed during the afternoon hours across South Texas triggering thunderstorms.  An upper level shortwave rotated out of Mexico during the afternoon providing increasing large-scale ascent, divergence aloft and steepening mid-level lapse rates.  Thunderstorms initially began as supercells across the Rio Grande Plains and Duval and Jim Wells counties during the afternoon and early evening, producing large hail and heavy rain.  The supercells organized into a squall-line during the evening and moved east across the Coastal Bend, producing heavy rainfall and flash flooding.  A wake low formed over the Coastal Bend behind the squall line as it moved into the offshore waters during the late night and early morning hours.  High sustained winds of 40 to 50 mph, with some gusts over 60 mph, developed over the Coastal Bend, Victoria Crossroads region and the bays and nearshore waters.  Damage associated with these winds was mainly confined to tree limbs, however a tug boat in Port Oconnor was reportedly damaged.  See High Wind event entry as well as wind entries under Gulf of Mexico for further information.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An intense low pressure moved across the northern tier of states during the day on the 27th. The low pressure system responsible for the heavy rain developed in the western Gulf of Mexico on the 5th. It moved northeast reaching the Tennessee Valley on the evening of the 5th and into the Great Lakes on the morning of the 6th. Its associated warm front moved north from the Carolinas on the morning of the 6th into the lower Delmarva Peninsula during the afternoon of the 6th before stalling. The occluded front associated with the primary low pressure system (It went northeast from the Great Lakes through the Saint Lawrence River Valley) moved through the region during the evening of the 6th and ended the rain. Precipitation initially started as a wintry mix before sunrise on the 6th and changed over to plain rain during the morning of the 6th.

Most of the accumulations were on grassy surfaces except for extreme northwest New Jersey where some slushy snow accumulated on secondary and tertiary roads. Precipitation began as rain around midnight EST on the 8th. As the low pressure system intensified off the Delmarva Peninsula and precipitation fell heavier, the rain changed to snow in most areas between 3 a.m. and 5 a.m. EST. When the precipitation intensity weakened at the end of the event, in some places the snow changed back to rain before ending by noon EST. A new low pressure system formed on the triple point of this occluded front over the Delmarva coastal waters during the early morning of the 8th. It intensified rapidly, but was also moving offshore quickly. Before it moved far enough offshore, it gave the northern half of New Jersey several hours of accumulating snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of Sunday, April 25th, heavy rain inundated the southern Coastal Bend of Texas.  A cold front became nearly stationary from near Victoria to Alice during the early morning hours of the 25th. A surface low formed across Deep South Texas and slowly tracked northeast. Analysis revealed strong easterly gulf inflow on the north side of the low, resulting in strong mass moisture convergence along the stalled front across the Southern Coastal Bend. Showers and thunderstorms began to form over Kleberg and Kenedy counties around 2 a.m. These storms intensified and moved north into western Nueces and San Patricio counties through 3 a.m. From 3 a.m. to 5 a.m. additional thunderstorms developed across Kleberg county and southern Nueces county and moved northeast across the Corpus Christi metro area. By 5 a.m the heaviest rainfall stretched from Taft to downtown Corpus Christi to Chapman Ranch. National Weather Service (NWS) Doppler radar estimated rainfall rates close to 2 inches per hour across this area. From 5 a.m. to 9 a.m. thunderstorms continued to reform over the south side of Corpus Christi and move northeast across the city, resulting in a training of storms. The heaviest showers and thunderstorms eventually tapered off and moved east between 10 a.m. and noon. NWS radar estimated widespread 5 to 8 inches of rainfall across most of Nueces and San Patricio counties east of U.S. 77. A bull's eye of 7 to 10 inches of rainfall was estimated across much of the south side of Corpus Christi.The heavy rainfall produced extensive flooding of primary and secondary roads in much of Nueces and San Patricio counties. The Corpus Christi Police Department reported over 100 vehicles stalled in highwater in Corpus Christi, with some drivers needing to be rescued. The water reached into several homes in Tuloso-Midway and Taft as well as some homes across the south side of Corpus Christi. Numerous city streets and intersections were not passable due to the flooding. Flooding along Interstate 37 was also reported near Calallen, Five Points and Annaville, triggering closures and rescues of vehicle passengers.6.18" of rain fell at the Corpus Chrisiti International Airport, establishing a new daily rainfall record for April 25th.  This also brought the monthly total to 9.21", establishing a new rainfall record for the month of April. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of Sunday, April 25th, heavy rain inundated the southern Coastal Bend of Texas.  A cold front became nearly stationary from near Victoria to Alice during the early morning hours of the 25th. A surface low formed across Deep South Texas and slowly tracked northeast. Analysis revealed strong easterly gulf inflow on the north side of the low, resulting in strong mass moisture convergence along the stalled front across the Southern Coastal Bend. Showers and thunderstorms began to form over Kleberg and Kenedy counties around 2 a.m. These storms intensified and moved north into western Nueces and San Patricio counties through 3 a.m. From 3 a.m. to 5 a.m. additional thunderstorms developed across Kleberg county and southern Nueces county and moved northeast across the Corpus Christi metro area. By 5 a.m the heaviest rainfall stretched from Taft to downtown Corpus Christi to Chapman Ranch. National Weather Service (NWS) Doppler radar estimated rainfall rates close to 2 inches per hour across this area. From 5 a.m. to 9 a.m. thunderstorms continued to reform over the south side of Corpus Christi and move northeast across the city, resulting in a training of storms. The heaviest showers and thunderstorms eventually tapered off and moved east between 10 a.m. and noon. NWS radar estimated widespread 5 to 8 inches of rainfall across most of Nueces and San Patricio counties east of U.S. 77. A bull's eye of 7 to 10 inches of rainfall was estimated across much of the south side of Corpus Christi.The heavy rainfall produced extensive flooding of primary and secondary roads in much of Nueces and San Patricio counties. The Corpus Christi Police Department reported over 100 vehicles stalled in highwater in Corpus Christi, with some drivers needing to be rescued. The water reached into several homes in Tuloso-Midway and Taft as well as some homes across the south side of Corpus Christi. Numerous city streets and intersections were not passable due to the flooding. Flooding along Interstate 37 was also reported near Calallen, Five Points and Annaville, triggering closures and rescues of vehicle passengers.6.18" of rain fell at the Corpus Chrisiti International Airport, establishing a new daily rainfall record for April 25th.  This also brought the monthly total to 9.21", establishing a new rainfall record for the month of April. Hail reportedly covered the ground in Guthrie County, into parts of Dallas County.  During the later evening hours, the thunderstorms began to sink south and took on a bow echo type configuration, though the line was not a true bow echo.  High winds began to be reported with Cass County being hit the worst.  A swath of damage 7 miles long was reported from west of Lewis to southeast of Lewis.  Embedded in the winds was a small tornado.  The tornado touched down intermittently along the 7 mile path and destroyed or damaged several grain bins and downed numerous trees.  A large corn crib was destroyed southeast of Atlantic and there were numerous reports of trees over highways.  In addition to the hail and high winds, heavy rain occurred from central into parts of west central Iowa.  Flash flooding occurred in Audubon, Guthrie, Madison, and Adair Counties.  Rain fell as the thunderstorms trained and redeveloped repeatedly over the same areas.  Rainfall rates were in the one to three inch per hour range with rainfall total reports of over 4 inches received in a few places in under two hours.  Water flooded over highways, even some U.S. Highways, to as depth of one to two feet.  This resulted in closure of some highways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving low pressure at both the surface and aloft produced periods of rain across Delaware from the morning of the 12th into the evening of the 13th. Two day storm totals averaged around 1.5 inches in New Castle County and 2.75 inches in Kent and Sussex Counties and caused poor drainage flooding and ponding of water in fields. Runoff from the heavy rain caused flooding along the Saint Jones River in Dover on the 14th. Specific storm totals included 3.10 inches in Milford (Kent County), 3.02 inches in Georgetown (Sussex County), 2.67 inches in Dover (Kent County), 2.54 inches in Greenwood and 1.53 inches in Wilmington (New Castle County). The low pressure system responsible for the heavy rain moved from Mississippi the morning of the 12th slowly northeast into Alabama during the evening of the 12th, extreme eastern Tennessee on the morning of the 13th, near Philadelphia early in the evening of the 13th and reached the Berkshires of Massachusetts just after midnight EDT on the 14th. The slow movement permitted this low pressure system to gather moisture from both the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic Ocean and dropped it onto the Middle Atlantic States.

Weak mid-level winds resulted in slow moving storms across these counties, with the storms merging and becoming nearly stationary along the Bee and Goliad county line.  Clearing skies across the Rio Grande Plains and Mexico during the afternoon led to increasing low-level instability.  A second mid and upper level shortwave rotated out of Mexico during the afternoon.  Thunderstorms developed from La Salle into Webb county during the afternoon hours with a few becoming severe.  The thunderstorms organized into a squall line during the evening moving east into the Coastal Bend.  The line weakend as it moved into a more stable airmass across the east, but did produce additional heavy rainfall and flash flooding across Bee, Goliad and San Patrcio counties.  Radar estimates 5 to 8 inches may have fallen along the Bee and Goliad county line with 3 to 5 inches elsewhere across the county.  Additionally 4 to 6 inches was estimated across southern La Salle county, however no flooding was reported.  Elsewhere 1 to 3 inches fell across portions of Live Oak, Northern Goliad, Western Refugio, Western San Patricio and Victoria counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A nearly stationary thunderstorm along the Bee and Goliad county line produced very heavy rainfall for several hours over the town of Berclair. (see episode narrative below for estimated rainfall amounts)  Law enforcement reported water over U.S. 59 near Berclair in far southwest Goliad county.

Ice Jams formed on the Colville River due to rapid warmup in the Brooks Range, and caused flooding near the village of Nuiqsut and the coastal plain to the Colville River Delta. At Nuiqsut flood waters went over the road to the old airport; the town itself was not flooded nor were there major impacts to the town. Nonetheless, the water was 15 to 20 feet high, and was the worst residents had seen in 30 years.  At Alpine Camp, a oil-drilling facility, floodwaters came to within 16 inches of the main pipeline. Water rose to within 14 inches of the lowest point of the access road  connecting two drilling pads, which sit on gravel 4 to 6 feet above the ground. On the Colville Delta, a family residence located on an island there had half of the island covered with water, including the airstrip which was fully underwater.  The above details were printed in the Anchorage Daily News.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist, and unstable airmass was in place over Iowa.  The warm front that had produced the convection during the early morning hours of the 8th had become stationary over northern Iowa.  With lifted indices below -10 C. over central Iowa and continued strong moisture advection, thunderstorms erupted over the central and northeast parts of the state during the late afternoon and evening hours.  For the most part, the thunderstorms produced hail during this event.  There were numerous reports of hail of one to two inches in diameter.  Hail reportedly covered the ground in Guthrie County, into parts of Dallas County.  During the later evening hours, the thunderstorms began to sink south and took on a bow echo type configuration, though the line was not a true bow echo.  High winds began to be reported with Cass County being hit the worst.  A swath of damage 7 miles long was reported from west of Lewis to southeast of Lewis.  Embedded in the winds was a small tornado.  The tornado touched down intermittently along the 7 mile path and destroyed or damaged several grain bins and downed numerous trees.  A large corn crib was destroyed southeast of Atlantic and there were numerous reports of trees over highways.  In addition to the hail and high winds, heavy rain occurred from central into parts of west central Iowa.  Flash flooding occurred in Audubon, Guthrie, Madison, and Adair Counties.  Rain fell as the thunderstorms trained and redeveloped repeatedly over the same areas.  Rainfall rates were in the one to three inch per hour range with rainfall total reports of over 4 inches received in a few places in under two hours.  Water flooded over highways, even some U.S. Highways, to as depth of one to two feet.  This resulted in closure of some highways.

Very strong south-southwest winds developed with profilers indicating wind of 50 to 65 kts within the lowest range gates.  Temperatures warmed into the mid 80s to low 90s with the atmosphere becoming adiabatic to between 750 and 600 mb, allowing for strong mixing down to the surface. A moist and unstable airmass was in place over Iowa during the afternoon of the 19th.  A southerly flow in the low levels brought dew point temperatures of the low 70s F. into southern Iowa.  This moist air was being pushed over a warm frontal boundary that lifted northeast across the state.  The airmass became capped over much of the state during the afternoon with a 2.4 degree C. cap in place over southwest Iowa by the early evening.  A small cluster of thunderstorms formed over northwest Iowa during the mid to late afternoon hours.  The storms moved east across the northern tier of Iowa Counties during the late afternoon and evening hours.  They produced hail of three quarters of an inch to an inch in diameter and wind gusts to around 60 MPH.  At one point the storm spiked in intensity.  It produced one and one half inch diameter hail as it passed southwest of Lakota in Kossuth County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very late season winter weather event hit northern North Dakota on May 11th and May 12th. Surface low pressure tracked farther south than expected and allowed cold air to filter into northern North Dakota out of Canada. Eight to 12 inches of snowfall was reported over the two day period with snow depths of two to six inches. Water equivalent in the snow was one to two inches. About two-thirds of Mountrail County was without power for at least part of the event as at least 150 power poles began failing as early as 4:00 pm CST on the 11th. One-thousand  customers were left without power. Hardest hit areas were Berthold, Des Lacs, South Prairie, Max and Carpio.

Strong cross winds may have been indirectly responsible for the death of a motorcyclist who lost control and crashed in a farm field in the Town of Yorkville of Racine County. Electrical companies estimated that about 20,000 customers in south-central and southeast Wisconsin lost power at one time or another.

A very warm and unstable airmass was in place over Iowa.  The moisture was in limited supply with this event.  A cold front approached the state from the northwest.  This front moved into the state during the late afternoon and evening of the 16th.  Moisture was limited with this system.  Surface dew points were in the mid 50s to around 60 during the early part of the afternoon over the southeast half of the state.  The moisture was very shallow.  Afternoon mixing lowered dew points into the upper 40s over the southeast, and into the upper 20s and 30s over the northwest just ahead of the front.  Temperatures warmed into mid 80s to low 90s which made the airmass quite unstable.  CAPE values were around 1000 J/kg with Lifted Indices around -4 C. just ahead of the front.  Convection had a hard time getting organized at first with only spotty cells forming ahead of the front.  By early evening, a small MCS formed over western Iowa and advanced east-southeast across the state.  The MCS produced hail in many locations along with gusty winds.  In spite of the "inverted V" type upper air soundings, high winds were not as widespread as would normally be expected.  Several locations did report gusts to around 60 MPH.  High winds blew a car off of Interstate 80 in Poweshiek County southeast of Malcom.  A wind gust of 70 MPH was reported at the Ames Airport in Story County.  For the most part, the hail was in the three quarter to one inch diameter size.  Hail did cover the ground in Carroll County at Lidderdale.  The largest hail report came from Guthrie County north of Panora into the Panora area.  Golf ball size hail was reported at that location.  There were several reports of gutter damage and dents in car hoods due to the hail in Panora.  Overall, damage was limited with this event since tree leaves were only beginning to come out and the crops had not yet been planted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very warm and unstable airmass was in place over Iowa.  The moisture was in limited supply with this event.  A cold front approached the state from the northwest.  This front moved into the state during the late afternoon and evening of the 16th.  Moisture was limited with this system.  Surface dew points were in the mid 50s to around 60 during the early part of the afternoon over the southeast half of the state.  The moisture was very shallow.  Afternoon mixing lowered dew points into the upper 40s over the southeast, and into the upper 20s and 30s over the northwest just ahead of the front.  Temperatures warmed into mid 80s to low 90s which made the airmass quite unstable.  CAPE values were around 1000 J/kg with Lifted Indices around -4 C. just ahead of the front.  Convection had a hard time getting organized at first with only spotty cells forming ahead of the front.  By early evening, a small MCS formed over western Iowa and advanced east-southeast across the state.  The MCS produced hail in many locations along with gusty winds.  In spite of the "inverted V" type upper air soundings, high winds were not as widespread as would normally be expected.  Several locations did report gusts to around 60 MPH.  High winds blew a car off of Interstate 80 in Poweshiek County southeast of Malcom.  A wind gust of 70 MPH was reported at the Ames Airport in Story County.  For the most part, the hail was in the three quarter to one inch diameter size.  Hail did cover the ground in Carroll County at Lidderdale.  The largest hail report came from Guthrie County north of Panora into the Panora area.  Golf ball size hail was reported at that location.  There were several reports of gutter damage and dents in car hoods due to the hail in Panora.  Overall, damage was limited with this event since tree leaves were only beginning to come out and the crops had not yet been planted.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The synoptic situation was very similar to what it was the previous day.  A complex weather situation was in place due to the convection from the previous night.  An outflow boundary extended east to west across northern Missouri.  The synoptic frontal boundary extended from central Nebraska across northern Iowa.  The air was clear over Iowa during the day, allowing for temperatures to recover.  Dew point values also recovered quite rapidly with readings in the upper 60s to low 70s by the late afternoon hours.  Lifted indices dropped into the -5 to -10 C. range by evening with CAPE values approaching 5000 J/kg.  By the evening hours, the frontal boundary and outflow boundary had converged and were located along Interstate 80.  Explosive thunderstorm development took place during the very late afternoon and evening hours in spite of the weak shear profile.  Discrete supercells formed in a narrow line along Interstate 80 from near Des Moines on west.  The storms became tornadic quickly.  To add insult to injury, a strong thunderstorm complex formed over Nebraska and moved east along the line of convection over Iowa.  As the event took shape, all modes of severe weather occurred.  The storms developed so rapidly that there was little more than a half hour from the first hail and wind report to the first tornado touchdown.  Hail and high wind reports were too numerous to mention individually here.  Numerous reports of golf ball size hail were received.  Boone and Story Counties reported some of the largest hail with the event as baseball size hail pelted the are.  There was one report of very large hail northwest of Slater in Story County.  Hail five and one half inches in diameter punched 8 holes through a steel roof.  There was severe house siding and roof damage in the area.  There were numerous tornadoes, especially in the central Iowa Iowa.  At one point there were several supercells around the metropolitan Des Moines area.  Two of the stronger tornadoes touched down west and south of Des Moines.  Fortunately, most of the tornado tracks were over open areas and resulted in little damage.  High winds became a problem, especially after sunset, as the complex from Nebraska moved in.  The system became more of a derecho during the late night hours.  Eighty plus MPH winds pelted southwest Iowa and downed barns and several buildings in Adams and Cass Counties.  A beta bow element formed in central Iowa shortly before midnight.  The bow echo produced a measured wind gust of 106 MPH in northern Warren County.  The high winds continued to push east along Interstate 80 for the next hour or so before it started to weaken.  The other major problem was with heavy rain.  The convection from the previous night set the stage by saturating soils.  The echos trained for several hours across central Iowa with very heavy rainfall.  Rainfall rates of 4 to 5 inches per hour were common under the heavier cells.  Several locations received 2 to 5 inch rainfalls in under  two hours, resulting in widespread flash flooding.  Reports of major highways being inundated by water were common.  By the end of the night, a swath of 4 to 9 inch rainfall was evident north of Interstate 80.  Longer term river flooding became a major problem by the morning of the 23rd.  There were two lightning related injuries.  Two people were injured when they were struck by lightning out of doors in Nevada.  The lightning struck close by as they were carrying groceries into their home.  The jolt caused them to fall, resulting in laceration to the head.

An intense low pressure moved across the northern tier of states during the day on the 27th.  Very strong south-southwest winds developed with profilers indicating wind of 50 to 65 kts within the lowest range gates.  Temperatures warmed into the mid 80s to low 90s with the atmosphere becoming adiabatic to between 750 and 600 mb, allowing for strong mixing down to the surface.  Winds increased during the day and reached high wind criteria by the early afternoon.  Most of the state saw sustained winds of 40 MPH or higher.  Several locations gusting to between 60 and 65 MPH.  The winds also produced blowing dust around the state.  Isolated reports of visibility reduced to near zero were received.  Spotty damage occurred around the state.  An 18 inch tree limb broke off and fell through the roof of a house in Windsor Heights.  A two to three foot diameter tree was snapped off at the base in Ames.  There were numerous reports of power outages caused by downed tree limbs.  In Union County, a 200 X 40 foot chicken house had the roof blown off.  There were several head of cattle in addition to the chickens contained therein trapped in the debris.

[Excessive rain fell on the 27th into the 28th over portions of northeast and east central North Dakota.  The Mayville, ND, radar showed most of the precipitation centered over the Devils Lake basin, with lesser amounts falling outward from that area.  Exact rainfall amounts were hard to come by, as many field observers did not have their raingauges up yet.  Also, neither the NDAWN (NDSU) or ARB (ND Atmospheric Resources Board) precipitation networks were active.  These networks are usually not activated until early April.  Therefore, the only amounts reported were generally from official NWS cooperative observers, who are not a very dense network (usually about 1 per county).  These cooperative observers reported amounts up to about 2.50 inches across the Cooperstown, Petersburg, Devils Lake, Cavalier, Adams, and Grafton areas.  However, people in the heavier rain area did report buckets or objects outside with upwards of 3 to 4 inches of rain in them.  Therefore, rain amounts were generally estimated to be in the 1 to 5 inch range across northeast and east central ND.  Being late March, soil surface and subsurface temperatures were around and mostly below freezing.  Areas along and north of US Highway 2 still had some snow cover, which was readily apparent on visible satellite imagery in the days leading up to this event.  The warm rain falling on top of snow led to even more water being released.  Snow depths and water equivalents are usually performed by official NWS cooperative observers every monday in the spring, while there is still snow on the ground.  On the previous monday (the 22nd), Cooperstown reported a snow water equivalent of 2.85 inches and Cavalier reported a snow water equivalent of 1.96 inches.  Some melting had occurred in the days leading up to March 27th, but most of this water was still in place as ice or snow.  Snow depths on the 27th ranged from a trace to 9-14 inches around the Langdon area.  Along with the frozen ground temperatures, river channels in the area still had their winter ice covering left.  This led to an ice jam threat.  Snow and ice also clogged culverts and drainage ditches.  Temperatures on the 27th were above freezing, mostly in the 40s over the heavy rain area, while southeast ND rose into the mid 60s.  Temperatures stayed above freezing until the morning of the 29th, but even this was too late to slow the moving water.]  For Ramsey county, there was basement flooding at several homes in the city of Devils Lake.  Crary reported 3 flooded buildings and a flooded city park.  Overland flooding was rampant around the Webster area, where water flowed over roads nearly all directions from town.  County-wide, one farmstead was completely cutoff and a total of 12 roads were blocked off.  Coulees feeding into Devils Lake ran above capacity.  Devils Lake started rising immediately.  The lake level was around 1446.56 feet on the 27th.  By the 28th, the level increased to 1446.76 feet.  Then, from the 28th on, the lake continued a steady rise toward the previous high of 1448.30 feet (which occurred on July 21, 2001).  Projections were for this previous high to be exceeded.  Flooding above this previous high is projected to be extremely expensive, with each foot of additional rise expected to cause about $30 million in damages.

A warm, moist, and unstable airmass was in place over Iowa.  The warm front that had produced the convection during the early morning hours of the 8th had become stationary over northern Iowa.  With lifted indices below -10 C. over central Iowa and continued strong moisture advection, thunderstorms erupted over the central and northeast parts of the state during the late afternoon and evening hours.  For the most part, the thunderstorms produced hail during this event.  There were numerous reports of hail of one to two inches in diameter.  Hail reportedly covered the ground in Guthrie County, into parts of Dallas County.  During the later evening hours, the thunderstorms began to sink south and took on a bow echo type configuration, though the line was not a true bow echo.  High winds began to be reported with Cass County being hit the worst.  A swath of damage 7 miles long was reported from west of Lewis to southeast of Lewis.  Embedded in the winds was a small tornado.  The tornado touched down intermittently along the 7 mile path and destroyed or damaged several grain bins and downed numerous trees.  A large corn crib was destroyed southeast of Atlantic and there were numerous reports of trees over highways.  In addition to the hail and high winds, heavy rain occurred from central into parts of west central Iowa.  Flash flooding occurred in Audubon, Guthrie, Madison, and Adair Counties.  Rain fell as the thunderstorms trained and redeveloped repeatedly over the same areas.  Rainfall rates were in the one to three inch per hour range with rainfall total reports of over 4 inches received in a few places in under two hours.  Water flooded over highways, even some U.S. Highways, to as depth of one to two feet.  This resulted in closure of some highways.

A couple of bursts of heavier rain interspersed within about thirty hours of nearly steady rain caused flooding along parts of the Millstone River in Somerset County. The rain began late in the evening on the 25th and ended before dawn on the 27th. Storm totals included 1.77 inches in Somerville and 1.60 inches in Bound Brook and North Plainfield. The Millstone River in Griggstown was above its 10 foot flood stage from 141 a.m. EDT on the 27th through 103 a.m. EDT on the 28th. The Griggstown Causeway was closed. The steady rain preceded a warm front that moved northeast from the Tennessee Valley through New Jersey on the 26th. It was followed quickly by a cold frontal passage later that day.

A slow moving low pressure at both the surface and aloft produced periods of rain across the Eastern Shore from the morning of the 12th into the evening of the 13th. The heaviest bursts of rain fell during the afternoons of the 12th and 13th. Two day storm totals averaged around two inches and caused poor drainage flooding and ponding of water in fields. Specific storm totals included 2.79 inches in Easton (Talbot County), 2.50 inches in Federalsburg (Caroline County) and 1.85 inches in Stevensville (Queen Anne's County). The low pressure system responsible for the heavy rain moved from Mississippi the morning of the 12th slowly northeast into Alabama during the evening of the 12th, extreme eastern Tennessee on the morning of the 13th, near Philadelphia early in the evening of the 13th and reached the Berkshires of Massachusetts just after midnight EDT on the 14th. The slow movement permitted this low pressure system to gather moisture from both the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic Ocean and dropped it onto the Middle Atlantic States.

The combination of heavy rain and snow melt caused poor drainage flooding across central and southern New Jersey. Some creek and river flooding also occurred. An intense low pressure moved across the northern tier of states during the day on the 27th.  Very strong south-southwest winds developed with profilers indicating wind of 50 to 65 kts within the lowest range gates.  Temperatures warmed into the mid 80s to low 90s with the atmosphere becoming adiabatic to between 750 and 600 mb, allowing for strong mixing down to the surface.  Winds increased during the day and reached high wind criteria by the early afternoon.  Most of the state saw sustained winds of 40 MPH or higher.  Several locations gusting to between 60 and 65 MPH.  The winds also produced blowing dust around the state.  Isolated reports of visibility reduced to near zero were received.  Spotty damage occurred around the state.  An 18 inch tree limb broke off and fell through the roof of a house in Windsor Heights.  A two to three foot diameter tree was snapped off at the base in Ames.  There were numerous reports of power outages caused by downed tree limbs.  In Union County, a 200 X 40 foot chicken house had the roof blown off.  There were several head of cattle in addition to the chickens contained therein trapped in the debris.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant severe weather event affected Texas and Oklahoma on the 3rd and 4th of March. Elevated severe thunderstorms first erupted across West Texas and far southeast New Mexico late in the evening on the 3rd. The activity increased in intensity and coverage through the night over the Permian Basin and Trans Pecos regions of Texas as a warm front moved north to the Interstate 20 corridor. Widely scattered supercell storms moved along the boundary over the southeast Permian Basin during the very early morning hours.  The convection then evolved into a broken squall line as it began to quickly spread east.  Several bookend vortices, line echo wave patterns, and bow segments were observed in the Doppler radar imagery across the eastern Permian Basin. A total of four weak tornadoes were confirmed to be associated with these signatures.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High gradient winds resulted in minor roof damage to a few light structures in Odessa. The strongest sustained wind speed measured across the Permian Basin during the late afternoon was 39 MPH at the Midland International Airport. It is estimated that sustained winds around 45 MPH caused the damage.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast-moving, broken, line of thunderstorms moved northeast through Rock, Walworth, and Jefferson counties during the early morning hours of March 5, 2004.  Although the thunderstorm cells were compact on radar, their wet-microbursts generated locally, brief, powerful, straight-line winds of 50 to 65 knots (58-75 mph).  In the city of Clinton, half of a home's roof was torn off, and the resultant wind-generated debris then damaged a nearby garage and a pick-up truck.  Otherwise the powerful winds uprooted large trees or cracked large tree limbs, or toppled power lines/power poles.

Breaks in the cloud cover allowed daytime heating to generate early-season, severe thunderstorms across south-central and southeast Wisconsin.  Although large hail up to 1.50 inches in diameter was the primary type of severe weather, there were scattered reports of powerful straight-line thunderstorm winds to around 52 kts (60 mph) which toppled trees and/or power lines.  The ground was "covered white" with hail southeast of Reedsburg (Sauk Co.) and in Sullivan (Jefferson Co.).  Synoptically, a low pressure and associated warm front moved northeast through southern Wisconsin, setting the stage for thunderstorm activity.  Maximum daytime temperatures were in the mid 50s to lower 60s.

A fast-moving, broken, line of thunderstorms moved northeast through Rock, Walworth, and Jefferson counties during the early morning hours of March 5, 2004.  Although the thunderstorm cells were compact on radar, their wet-microbursts generated locally, brief, powerful, straight-line winds of 50 to 65 knots (58-75 mph).  In the city of Clinton, half of a home's roof was torn off, and the resultant wind-generated debris then damaged a nearby garage and a pick-up truck.  Otherwise the powerful winds uprooted large trees or cracked large tree limbs, or toppled power lines/power poles.

A strong low pressure system lifted northeast across Northern Lower Michigan on the afternoon of the 5th. Across Eastern Upper Michigan, six to ten inch accumulations were common, with the highest amounts in western Mackinac County near Naubinway.

Snow began in Eastern Iowa during the morning of 15 March and became heavy in the late afternoon and overnight hours.  The snow tapered to flurries just before dawn on 16 March and ended by mid-morning.  Mesoscale banding of snow produced a band of 10+ inches that was 1-2 counties wide.  Final snowfall amounts included Brighton, Iowa 16 inches; Sigourney, Iowa 14.3 inches; Columbus Jct and Wapello 12 and 11.5 inches respectively; North English and Washington 12 and 10.2 inches respectively; and Mediapolis, Iowa 10 inches.  Another very narrow mesoscale band of snow produced 6-7 inches of snow in just over 12 hours from Lowden, to Wheatland, to Park View, Iowa across parts of Cedar, Clinton, and Scott counties.

A late winter storm dropped heavy snow in Northwestern New Jersey, a wintry mix in the Raritan Basin and the rest of the northern half of New Jersey and snow to rain across the eastern Philadelphia suburbs on the 16th. Numerous accidents occurred and traffic was snarled on Interstates 80 and 287 and U.S Routes 1 and 9 in the northern half of the state. As warmer air moved in from the Atlantic Ocean, precipitation changed to rain in the greater Philadelphia Metropolitan Area during the early afternoon of the 16th. A warm, moist, and unstable airmass was in place over Iowa.  The warm front that had produced the convection during the early morning hours of the 8th had become stationary over northern Iowa.  With lifted indices below -10 C. over central Iowa and continued strong moisture advection, thunderstorms erupted over the central and northeast parts of the state during the late afternoon and evening hours.  For the most part, the thunderstorms produced hail during this event.  There were numerous reports of hail of one to two inches in diameter.  Hail reportedly covered the ground in Guthrie County, into parts of Dallas County.  During the later evening hours, the thunderstorms began to sink south and took on a bow echo type configuration, though the line was not a true bow echo.  High winds began to be reported with Cass County being hit the worst.  A swath of damage 7 miles long was reported from west of Lewis to southeast of Lewis.  Embedded in the winds was a small tornado.  The tornado touched down intermittently along the 7 mile path and destroyed or damaged several grain bins and downed numerous trees.  A large corn crib was destroyed southeast of Atlantic and there were numerous reports of trees over highways.  In addition to the hail and high winds, heavy rain occurred from central into parts of west central Iowa.  Flash flooding occurred in Audubon, Guthrie, Madison, and Adair Counties.  Rain fell as the thunderstorms trained and redeveloped repeatedly over the same areas.  Rainfall rates were in the one to three inch per hour range with rainfall total reports of over 4 inches received in a few places in under two hours.  Water flooded over highways, even some U.S. Highways, to as depth of one to two feet.  This resulted in closure of some highways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong early spring storm moving from the Four Corners region into northeast Colorado brought copious amounts of snow.  Some of the higher snow totals include the following...6 to 10 inches northwest of Canon City in Fremont county...at Antonito in Conejos county...in the Black Forest area of northern El Paso county...around Florissant in Teller county...around Kim in eastern Las Animas county...and in the Creede area of Mineral county...12 to 18 inches at Buena Vista in Chaffee county...near Divide in Teller county...around Woodland Park in Teller county...around Trinidad in Las Animas county... around Westcliffe in Custer county...around Del Norte in Rio Grande county...and at Maysville in Chaffee county... 2 feet around Beulah and Rye in Pueblo county...west and northwest of Westcliffe in Custer county...31 inches at La Veta...and in the Walsenburg area in Huerfano county...34 inches inundated the area 6 miles north-northwest of Aguilar...and the highest reported snow amount at Cuchara in Huerfano county with 38 inches.  Several of the locations that received in excess of 24 inches of snow...also had water equivalents in excess of 3 inches.  There were numerous power outages in the heaviest snow areas...including the Wet Mountain Valley around Westcliffe where power was lost from 12 hours to 4 days. An intense low pressure moved across the northern tier of states during the day on the 27th.  Very strong south-southwest winds developed with profilers indicating wind of 50 to 65 kts within the lowest range gates.  Temperatures warmed into the mid 80s to low 90s with the atmosphere becoming adiabatic to between 750 and 600 mb, allowing for strong mixing down to the surface.  Winds increased during the day and reached high wind criteria by the early afternoon.  Most of the state saw sustained winds of 40 MPH or higher.  Several locations gusting to between 60 and 65 MPH.  The winds also produced blowing dust around the state.  Isolated reports of visibility reduced to near zero were received.  Spotty damage occurred around the state.  An 18 inch tree limb broke off and fell through the roof of a house in Windsor Heights.  A two to three foot diameter tree was snapped off at the base in Ames.  There were numerous reports of power outages caused by downed tree limbs.  In Union County, a 200 X 40 foot chicken house had the roof blown off.  There were several head of cattle in addition to the chickens contained therein trapped in the debris.

The storm system on the 18th produced heavy rainfall as well as severe thunderstorms. As the low moved from the plains into the Upper Great Lakes, warm and very moist air from the Gulf of Mexico spread northeast as well. Heavy rain under the stronger storms left standing water in yards and parking lots. This first round of convection diminished during the afternoon as the storms moved east. The approach of the low pressure system's cold front then set the stage for another round of thunderstorms in the late evening on the 18th. Heavy rain also fell under the most intense thunderstorms. Total rainfall amounts  were excessive at many places west of Marquette and Iron Mountain. Marenisco in Gogebic County was inundated with 2.90 inches of rain. Some other impressive rainfall totals include 2.64 inches at Ironwood, 2.57 inches at Pelkie,  2.20 inches at Amasa, 2.07 inches at Baraga, and 2.00 inches at Watton.   This heavy rainfall caused some minor flooding of smaller streams and low-lying areas. The runoff from the precipitation and the melting of lingering snow over the higher terrain areas caused some flooding of the larger rivers over the west half of Upper Michigan that lingered for several days after the rain ended. Temperatures warmed into the mid 80s to low 90s with the atmosphere becoming adiabatic to between 750 and 600 mb, allowing for strong mixing down to the surface.  Winds increased during the day and reached high wind criteria by the early afternoon.  Most of the state saw sustained winds of 40 MPH or higher.  Several locations gusting to between 60 and 65 MPH.  The winds also produced blowing dust around the state.  Isolated reports of visibility reduced to near zero were received.  Spotty damage occurred around the state.  An 18 inch tree limb broke off and fell through the roof of a house in Windsor Heights.  A two to three foot diameter tree was snapped off at the base in Ames.  There were numerous reports of power outages caused by downed tree limbs.  In Union County, a 200 X 40 foot chicken house had the roof blown off.  There were several head of cattle in addition to the chickens contained therein trapped in the debris.

The airmass remained unstable over Iowa through the mid day hours of the 30th.  The cold front mentioned above had not yet passed through the state.  At the same time, a mesoscale low pressure system lifted north into the state by mid day.  Thunderstorms erupted along the eastern periphery of the low and became marginally severe over parts of southeast Iowa.  Three quarter inch diameter hail fell in Wapello and Appanoose Counties as the narrow line of storms passed.

The synoptic situation was very similar to what it was the previous day.  A complex weather situation was in place due to the convection from the previous night.  An outflow boundary extended east to west across northern Missouri.  The synoptic frontal boundary extended from central Nebraska across northern Iowa.  The air was clear over Iowa during the day, allowing for temperatures to recover.  Dew point values also recovered quite rapidly with readings in the upper 60s to low 70s by the late afternoon hours.  Lifted indices dropped into the -5 to -10 C. range by evening with CAPE values approaching 5000 J/kg.  By the evening hours, the frontal boundary and outflow boundary had converged and were located along Interstate 80.  Explosive thunderstorm development took place during the very late afternoon and evening hours in spite of the weak shear profile.  Discrete supercells formed in a narrow line along Interstate 80 from near Des Moines on west.  The storms became tornadic quickly.  To add insult to injury, a strong thunderstorm complex formed over Nebraska and moved east along the line of convection over Iowa.  As the event took shape, all modes of severe weather occurred.  The storms developed so rapidly that there was little more than a half hour from the first hail and wind report to the first tornado touchdown.  Hail and high wind reports were too numerous to mention individually here.  Numerous reports of golf ball size hail were received.  Boone and Story Counties reported some of the largest hail with the event as baseball size hail pelted the are.  There was one report of very large hail northwest of Slater in Story County.  Hail five and one half inches in diameter punched 8 holes through a steel roof.  There was severe house siding and roof damage in the area.  There were numerous tornadoes, especially in the central Iowa Iowa.  At one point there were several supercells around the metropolitan Des Moines area.  Two of the stronger tornadoes touched down west and south of Des Moines.  Fortunately, most of the tornado tracks were over open areas and resulted in little damage.  High winds became a problem, especially after sunset, as the complex from Nebraska moved in.  The system became more of a derecho during the late night hours.  Eighty plus MPH winds pelted southwest Iowa and downed barns and several buildings in Adams and Cass Counties.  A beta bow element formed in central Iowa shortly before midnight.  The bow echo produced a measured wind gust of 106 MPH in northern Warren County.  The high winds continued to push east along Interstate 80 for the next hour or so before it started to weaken.  The other major problem was with heavy rain.  The convection from the previous night set the stage by saturating soils.  The echos trained for several hours across central Iowa with very heavy rainfall.  Rainfall rates of 4 to 5 inches per hour were common under the heavier cells.  Several locations received 2 to 5 inch rainfalls in under  two hours, resulting in widespread flash flooding.  Reports of major highways being inundated by water were common.  By the end of the night, a swath of 4 to 9 inch rainfall was evident north of Interstate 80.  Longer term river flooding became a major problem by the morning of the 23rd.  There were two lightning related injuries.  Two people were injured when they were struck by lightning out of doors in Nevada.  The lightning struck close by as they were carrying groceries into their home.  The jolt caused them to fall, resulting in laceration to the head.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Brief touchdown in open fields.

A winter storm moving southeast from the Gulf of Alaska, picked up tropical moisture before it moved onshore. The warmer air mass caused the snow level to remain high during most of the precipitaion event, so that measured snow fall was less than eight inches in the mountains. However strong winds did occur in the mountains and heavy rain fell over much of Southern California. Most roads along the foothills of the San Bernardino Mountains, both on the north and south side were closed due to flooding and mud slides. Also, over Orange County and San Diego County, several major highways and secondary roads were closed due to flooding.

Once again it was a very active severe weather day over Iowa.  The frontal system that had moved through the state on the night of the 22nd was returning north as a warm front.  This time Iowa did not get completely into the warm sector.  The surface front was dragged north into Iowa by low pressure that moved out of Kansas northeast into central Iowa by the mid to late evening.  The airmass was pushed southeast out of the state by a cold front that passed through the state during the evening and early morning hours.  The airmass in the warm sector became very unstable.  Lifted indices were around -13 C with CAPE values greater than 5000 J/kg by the late afternoon.  The air advected north into Iowa during the day and into the evening.  Thunderstorms erupted in two places.  The first to affect the DSM CWA was the development of several elevated supercells over west central into southwest Iowa.  The storms continued to lift east and northeast across the area.  A few tornadoes touched down, however with the very elevated nature of the storms it was very difficult for the tornadoes to reach the ground.  By the late afternoon, a solid squall line developed along the cold front.  The line took on a Line Echo Wave Pattern by evening.  Several segments of the line bowed out, resulting in high winds.  At times the winds reached 80 MPH.  One of the thunderstorms produced high winds in the Early area of Sac County.  They overturned a semi-tractortrailer truck, causing $80,000 damage and causing minor injuries to the driver.  Tornadoes that formed along this line actually formed where the Rear Flank Downdraft cut through the line.  A clear meso was formed and the small tornadoes advanced around the meso and were in front of the thunderstorm line.  Touchdowns were all brief.  Hail was common with the stronger storm, with much of it in the one to one and three-quarter inch in diameter.  Given the antecedent soil conditions in Iowa, flash flooding became a major issue.  Numerous counties reported flash flooding as rainfall of one to 4 inches in spots resulted in flooded highways.  The thunderstorms formed into an MCC by the early evening hours.  As they moved out of the state, they delivered one more punch to the state.  High winds developed in the wake of the complex.  Several counties of north central, northeast, and central Iowa received high winds.  Damage occurred in several locations to both trees and out buildings.  Sustained winds across the area were in the 25 to 45 MPH range with some higher gusts.  Clarion reported a wind gust of 63 MPH for the highest wind gust reported.

A fast-moving, broken, line of thunderstorms moved northeast through Rock, Walworth, and Jefferson counties during the early morning hours of March 5, 2004.  Although the thunderstorm cells were compact on radar, their wet-microbursts generated locally, brief, powerful, straight-line winds of 50 to 65 knots (58-75 mph).  In the city of Clinton, half of a home's roof was torn off, and the resultant wind-generated debris then damaged a nearby garage and a pick-up truck.  Otherwise the powerful winds uprooted large trees or cracked large tree limbs, or toppled power lines/power poles.

North and Central Georgia endured one of the driest March's on record.  With only near to slightly below normal rainfall during January and February, by the end of March, most of the area was classified in a mild drought.  Most areas of the state only received around one inch of rain during the entire month.  Climatologically, March is the wettest month of the year across most of the area.  Columbus recorded their driest March ever since records began in the late 1800s with only 0.56 inch of rain.  This is 5.19 inches below normal for the month.  The other major reporting sites all reported similar stories.  Atlanta received only 1.04 inches of rain, which is 4.34 inches below normal for the month and the third driest March since records began in the late 1800s.  Athens recorded only 1.05 inches of rain, which is 3.94 inches below normal for the month and the second driest March on record.  For Macon, only 0.43 inches of rain fell during the month, also marking it as the second driest March on record and leaving that site 4.47 inches below normal for the month.  In addition, with the exception of Macon, the January through March 2004 period ranked as being in the top driest 10 for this period since records began.

A strong low pressure system lifted northeast across Northern Lower Michigan on the afternoon of the 5th. The Pine River near Rudyard flooded due to an ice jam between Mackinac Trail and I-75.  A river stage of 19.3 feet was observed at Mackinac Trail, which established a new flood of record.  The old flood of record was 18.4 feet on March 30 1986.  The river submerged the Prairie Road bridge west of Rudyard, along with several other roads and yards in the vicinity. North and Central Georgia endured one of the driest March's on record.  With only near to slightly below normal rainfall during January and February, by the end of March, most of the area was classified in a mild drought.  Most areas of the state only received around one inch of rain during the entire month.  Climatologically, March is the wettest month of the year across most of the area.  Columbus recorded their driest March ever since records began in the late 1800s with only 0.56 inch of rain.  This is 5.19 inches below normal for the month.  The other major reporting sites all reported similar stories.  Atlanta received only 1.04 inches of rain, which is 4.34 inches below normal for the month and the third driest March since records began in the late 1800s.  Athens recorded only 1.05 inches of rain, which is 3.94 inches below normal for the month and the second driest March on record.  For Macon, only 0.43 inches of rain fell during the month, also marking it as the second driest March on record and leaving that site 4.47 inches below normal for the month.  In addition, with the exception of Macon, the January through March 2004 period ranked as being in the top driest 10 for this period since records began.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong gradient winds affected south-central and southeast Wisconsin for many hours.  Maximum wind  gusts were generally in the 40 to 49 kt range (46 to 57 mph).  There were numerous newspaper reports of broken tree branches hitting power lines with a resultant power outage.  Strong cross winds may have been indirectly responsible for the death of a motorcyclist who lost control and crashed in a farm field in the Town of Yorkville of Racine County.  In Sheboygan County near Glenbeulah the strong winds moved a silo off its foundation about 16 inches, ripped a door off a barn, and knocked down some large trees.  In the city of Sheboygan the strong winds blew in several windows at a car dealership.  Near the city of Oregon (Dane Co.) a home was damaged by a large, wind-toppled tree.  Electrical companies estimated that about 20,000 customers in south-central and southeast Wisconsin lost power at one time or another.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite temperatures in the 50s from a shallow marine layer, severe thunderstorms formed in southeast Massachusetts during the afternoon due to the presence of instability aloft.  A small line of thunderstorms dropped penny sized hail in Plymouth before weakening, then another thunderstorm on Cape Cod became severe and dropped penny sized hail in Mashpee.Another round of severe thunderstorms moved across Massachusetts during the evening ahead of a cold front.  There were many reports of large hail, especially in the Connecticut Valley, where hailstones as large as golf balls were observed in Greenfield.  Penny to quarter sized hail fell in parts of central and eastern Massachusetts, from Gardner to Clinton and Foxborough.  No damage was reported as a result of the large hail.Lightning from thunderstorms caused significant damage in parts of central and eastern Massachusetts.  Two homes in Andover and Needham sustained major damage as a result of lightning-induced fires, and minor damage to homes and a church was reported in Spencer, Lowell, Sharon, and Stoughton.

3 low-topped supercell thunderstorms dropped down at least 1 tornado a piece and a total of 6 tornadoes across Central Indiana during the late afternoon and early evening of April 20. All of the tornadoes were F0 or F1 in rating. The worst damage occurred in Kokomo as 3 homes were damaged and a skating rink and trucking company had significant damage totaling around 3 million dollars. There were also 1 minor injury. The town of Jamestown along the Hendricks/Boone county border also was hit hard with significant damage to a dozen homes totaling 1.65 million dollars.  There were also 8 minor injuries, 1 as a result of his semi being overturned along Interstate 74.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A second tornado, associated with a low-topped supercell that damaged homes in the Jamestown area, touched down in rural Boone county. Eyewitnesses reported funnel clouds and scattered damage along the path.

A major late season winter storm affected a portion of northeast Montana beginning late on the evening of the 10th, and continued until about noon on the 12th. The storm produced up to a foot of heavy wet snow, with snow drifts up to 5 feet deep. Low pressure developed in Wyoming on the evening of the 10th and tracked into the Dakotas during the afternoon hours of the 11th. Rain changed to snow late on the evening of the 10th and during the pre dawn hours of the 11th.  Periods of snow continued through the morning of the 12th, and some of the snow fell heavily at times during the day on the 11th. Snowfall ranged from about 3 inches to as much as a foot across most of northeast Montana north of the Missouri River.  Snowdrifts of up to 5 feet were reported in northern Valley County. In addition, strong east winds of 20 to 40 mph produced considerable blowing and drifting snow which reduced the visibility to less than a quarter of a mile at times.  Many schools were closed, and roads were open to emergency travel only in Central and Northern Valley County as well as Daniels and Sheridan Counties during the day on the 11th and into the early morning hours of the 12th. A warm, moist, and unstable airmass was in place over Iowa.  The warm front that had produced the convection during the early morning hours of the 8th had become stationary over northern Iowa.  With lifted indices below -10 C. over central Iowa and continued strong moisture advection, thunderstorms erupted over the central and northeast parts of the state during the late afternoon and evening hours.  For the most part, the thunderstorms produced hail during this event.  There were numerous reports of hail of one to two inches in diameter.  Hail reportedly covered the ground in Guthrie County, into parts of Dallas County.  During the later evening hours, the thunderstorms began to sink south and took on a bow echo type configuration, though the line was not a true bow echo.  High winds began to be reported with Cass County being hit the worst.  A swath of damage 7 miles long was reported from west of Lewis to southeast of Lewis.  Embedded in the winds was a small tornado.  The tornado touched down intermittently along the 7 mile path and destroyed or damaged several grain bins and downed numerous trees.  A large corn crib was destroyed southeast of Atlantic and there were numerous reports of trees over highways.  In addition to the hail and high winds, heavy rain occurred from central into parts of west central Iowa.  Flash flooding occurred in Audubon, Guthrie, Madison, and Adair Counties.  Rain fell as the thunderstorms trained and redeveloped repeatedly over the same areas.  Rainfall rates were in the one to three inch per hour range with rainfall total reports of over 4 inches received in a few places in under two hours.  Water flooded over highways, even some U.S. Highways, to as depth of one to two feet.  This resulted in closure of some highways.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained spotter reported 60 mile an hour winds and downed power lines near the intersection of 81st Street and 129th East Avenue.
Thunderstorm winds estimated at 70 miles an hour blew off half of garage's roof and tore some shingle off a home.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: May 2004 began rather dry with an average of only 0.19 inches of rain over the first week of the month.  However, the second week of May brought seasonally normal rainfall.  Heavy rain occurred during the third week of the month.  May's greatest rain events came back to back.  The first round of heavy rain producing thunderstorms began on the morning of the 21st and continued into the morning of the 22ns.  Heaviest rains were in North Central and Northeast Iowa where storm totals included 4.75 inches at Emmetsburg, 6.22 inches at Mason City, and 5.14 inches at Decorah.  Another round of storms began on the afternoon of the 22nd and continued into the morning of the 23rd.  Some of the rain totals reported with this second series of storms included 6.67 inches near Ames and 4.15 inches at Marshalltown.  A statewide average of 2.97 inches of rain fell from these two systems.  Locally heavy rain continued to fall through much of the remainder of the month.  The greatest rainfall amount occurred during the early morning hours of the 30th when 4.37 inches of rain fell at Fairfield.  Damage reports were still coming in but it does appear from preliminary reports that roughly six percent of Iowa's 2004 crop was flood out.  Based on a $23 per acre cost to replant it is estimated that the floods have cost Iowa farmers some $15.2 million dollars.  The rainfall that occurred over the later part of May was Iowa's greatest since July 1993.  Rainfall totals for the month varied form 4.01 inches at Burlington to 14.87 inches at Lansing.  Radar derived estimates suggest that May rainfall was actually below normal in some areas over the far Northwest...such as Buena Vista and Van Buren Counties.  However, complete rain gage reports were not yet available for these areas.  Excessive rainfall produced major flooding in many areas across the state during the second half of May.  This was the first widespread major flood event in many years.  The heaviest rainfall occurred over the Northeastern sections of the state.  Additionally, several episodes of severe thunderstorms produced large hail, high winds, and tornadoes during May.  Severe weather was reported on 15 days during the month with all but 7 of Iowa's 99 counties reporting severe thunderstorm events.  The month's largest severe weather outbreaks occurred on the 8th (26 counties, mostly west central to northeast) ; 17th (20 counties, mostly southwest to east central); 21st (37 counties, mostly northwest to east central); 22nd (31 counties, mostly southwest to east central) and the 24th (33 counties, mostly southwest one half).  An exact tornado count is not yet available for the state, but central Iowa did report 32 tornadoes for the month with an estimated total of 50 tornadoes statewide.  Nearly all were F0 and F1 intensity with minimal damage to communities.  There was a tornado of F2 intensity that did produce significant damage to the communities of Bradgate and Palo (both on May 21).

Severe weather was reported on 15 days during the month with all but 7 of Iowa's 99 counties reporting severe thunderstorm events.  The month's largest severe weather outbreaks occurred on the 8th (26 counties, mostly west central to northeast) ; 17th (20 counties, mostly southwest to east central); 21st (37 counties, mostly northwest to east central); 22nd (31 counties, mostly southwest to east central) and the 24th (33 counties, mostly southwest one half).  An exact tornado count is not yet available for the state, but central Iowa did report 32 tornadoes for the month with an estimated total of 50 tornadoes statewide.  Nearly all were F0 and F1 intensity with minimal damage to communities.  There was a tornado of F2 intensity that did produce significant damage to the communities of Bradgate and Palo (both on May 21).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A warm, moist, and unstable airmass was in place over Iowa.  The warm front that had produced the convection during the early morning hours of the 8th had become stationary over northern Iowa.  With lifted indices below -10 C. over central Iowa and continued strong moisture advection, thunderstorms erupted over the central and northeast parts of the state during the late afternoon and evening hours.  For the most part, the thunderstorms produced hail during this event.  There were numerous reports of hail of one to two inches in diameter.  Hail reportedly covered the ground in Guthrie County, into parts of Dallas County.  During the later evening hours, the thunderstorms began to sink south and took on a bow echo type configuration, though the line was not a true bow echo.  High winds began to be reported with Cass County being hit the worst.  A swath of damage 7 miles long was reported from west of Lewis to southeast of Lewis.  Embedded in the winds was a small tornado.  The tornado touched down intermittently along the 7 mile path and destroyed or damaged several grain bins and downed numerous trees.  A large corn crib was destroyed southeast of Atlantic and there were numerous reports of trees over highways.  In addition to the hail and high winds, heavy rain occurred from central into parts of west central Iowa.  Flash flooding occurred in Audubon, Guthrie, Madison, and Adair Counties.  Rain fell as the thunderstorms trained and redeveloped repeatedly over the same areas.  Rainfall rates were in the one to three inch per hour range with rainfall total reports of over 4 inches received in a few places in under two hours.  Water flooded over highways, even some U.S. Highways, to as depth of one to two feet.  This resulted in closure of some highways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Once again it was a very active severe weather day over Iowa.  The frontal system that had moved through the state on the night of the 22nd was returning north as a warm front.  This time Iowa did not get completely into the warm sector.  The surface front was dragged north into Iowa by low pressure that moved out of Kansas northeast into central Iowa by the mid to late evening.  The airmass was pushed southeast out of the state by a cold front that passed through the state during the evening and early morning hours.  The airmass in the warm sector became very unstable.  Lifted indices were around -13 C with CAPE values greater than 5000 J/kg by the late afternoon.  The air advected north into Iowa during the day and into the evening.  Thunderstorms erupted in two places.  The first to affect the DSM CWA was the development of several elevated supercells over west central into southwest Iowa.  The storms continued to lift east and northeast across the area. The low pressure mentioned in the narrative above tracked across South Dakota and Minnesota during the evening hours of the 18th.  The airmass, though quite unstable based on the soundings, was significantly capped over Iowa.  The Omaha sounding showed a Lifted Index around -7 C, with CAPE values around 1500 J/kg.  In spite of the instability, the cap over Iowa was quite strong with CIN values around 300 J/kg.  Thunderstorms erupted to the west of the area along a cold front as it entered the state.  Initially, the storms produced severe weather to the west of Iowa where the atmosphere was not as capped.  As the line moved into Iowa, it weakened due to the cap and the presence of much drier air.  Ironically, most of the storms produced lighter wind speeds as they passed than the ambient wind was prior to the storms approach.  Needless to say, this made the task of differentiation between thunderstorm winds and gradient high winds more difficult.  High winds were reported in a few areas.  Thunderstorm winds blew down a barn in Hancock County near Klemme, trapping several head of cattle under the barn.  Trees were also downed in the area.  The ASOS recorded a 58 MPH wind at the Mason City Airport as the storms moved through.  The storms did produce some small hail as they moved through.  Spotty reports showed hail was in the three quarter inch up to nickle size.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of heavy rain and snow melt caused poor drainage flooding across the Eastern Shore. The frozen ground caused considerable ponding of water in fields and in poor drainage areas. Heavier rain fell from the middle of the morning into the early evening on the 6th. Storm totals included 2.26 inches in Conowingo (Cecil County), 1.80 inches in Stevensville (Queen Anne's County), 1.45 inches in Easton (Talbot County) and 1.20 inches in Federalsburg (Caroline County). The low pressure system responsible for the heavy rain developed in the western Gulf of Mexico on the 5th. It moved northeast reaching the Tennessee Valley on the evening of the 5th and into the Great Lakes on the morning of the 6th. Its associated warm front moved north from the Carolinas on the morning of the 6th into the lower Delmarva Peninsula during the afternoon of the 6th before stalling. The occluded front associated with the primary low pressure system (It went northeast from the Great Lakes through the Saint Lawrence River Valley.) moved through the region during the night of the 6th and ended the rain. Precipitation initially began as a wintry mix during the late evening of the 5th across northern parts of the Eastern Shore before changing to rain during the morning of the 6th.
