EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very unstable situation took shape over Iowa during the day on the 11th.  A nearly stationary frontal boundary extended nearly east to west across the state along U.S. Highway 20, or roughly from Fort Dodge to Waterloo.  Very unstable air was to the south of the front with dew point temperatures in the low to mid 70s common.  By early afternoon, CAPE values were near 5000 J/KG with lifted indices in the -10 to -12 C. range.  A dry line advanced east toward the state along with the passage of a short wave lifting northeast across the area.  Thunderstorms fired along the triple point by the early afternoon hours in northwest Iowa.  The storms became severe very quickly and produced tornadoes as the sounding profile became very favorable.  In addition, significant mid level cooling took place as 700 mb temperatures fell several degrees during the day.   Most of the storms remained over the north third of the state with numerous reports of tornadoes.  The bulk of the tornadoes progressed southeast from northwest Iowa into the central counties of the state as the afternoon turned into evening.  For the most part, the tornadoes were quite small with only a few remaining on the ground for more than a few tenths of a mile.  Two tornadoes in Palo Alto and Emmet Counties were on the ground for a significant period of time, however they tracked over open country.  There were several tornadoes in Webster County.  Most of them were also small and did little damage, however one tornado near Otho hit two farmsteads there causing considerable damage.  One farmstead was nearly destroyed, including significant damage to the house.  Hail was common with the storms with much of it in the three quarter to one and one quarter inch diameter range.  There were a few golf ball size hail reports in Webster and Hamilton Counties, and one tennis ball size hail report in Stratford in Hamilton County.  Spotty reports of high were were received.  Winds were in the 60 to 70 MPH range.  Rainfall became a problem in a couple areas.  In Kossuth County rainfall of 2 to over 3 inches fell in under 2 hours causing flooding around the County.  Several roads became flooded, including Iowa Highway 9 and U.S. Highway 169.  Very heavy rain in the 2 to 4 inch range fell in Hamilton County during a 2 hour period.  This caused considerable flooding in the county, especially over the northwest half.  There was one high wind event.  In what turned out to be a high wind event occurred in Marion County.  A 60 MPH wind was recorded in Pella.  The event was in the wake of the line of thunderstorms and actually effected a several county area with winds of 40 to 50 MPH.  Temperatures shot up 9 degrees in a few minutes at the Des Moines Airport as a 51 MPH wind gust pushed the temperature up to 90 during the mid evening hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active and very complicated round of severe thunderstorms affected west Texas during the late afternoon and evening of the 5th. Severe weather development was focused in two areas of the region. Convective initiation occurred first near a sub-synoptic scale outflow boundary that was situated across the southeast Permian Basin. This feature was a remnant from overnight convection to the northeast of the area. Two supercell thunderstorms developed along the boundary over rural areas of southeast Midland and northern Upton Counties. As these storms moved east, storm-scale outflow boundaries were observed in local warning radar base reflectivity and velocity data arcing away from the storms toward the west. Both of these boundaries interacted with the larger scale baroclinic boundary under a field of strongly growing convective towers over southern and central Midland County and northeast Crane County. A series of at least four landspout tornadoes were observed as these interactions occurred.The mesoscale boundary began propagating west-northwest across the basin as the supercell storms provided convective enhancement to the cool (east) side of the boundary. Meanwhile strong to severe thunderstorms began propagating east from the mountainous areas of southeast New Mexico and southwest Texas. The convectively enhanced outflow boundary interacted with the complex of storms over the Upper Trans Pecos region. Large hail and two tornadoes were observed in east-central Reeves County.

Two supercell thunderstorms developed along the boundary over rural areas of southeast Midland and northern Upton Counties. As these storms moved east, storm-scale outflow boundaries were observed in local warning radar base reflectivity and velocity data arcing away from the storms toward the west. Both of these boundaries interacted with the larger scale baroclinic boundary under a field of strongly growing convective towers over southern and central Midland County and northeast Crane County. A series of at least four landspout tornadoes were observed as these interactions occurred.The mesoscale boundary began propagating west-northwest across the basin as the supercell storms provided convective enhancement to the cool (east) side of the boundary. Meanwhile strong to severe thunderstorms began propagating east from the mountainous areas of southeast New Mexico and southwest Texas. The convectively enhanced outflow boundary interacted with the complex of storms over the Upper Trans Pecos region. Large hail and two tornadoes were observed in east-central Reeves County.

Two major rainfall events during the last 10 days of May 2004 resulted in major to near record flooding across parts of East Central and Northeast Iowa that continued into June 2004.  Following is an edited write up from the Service Hydrologist:The first event occurred from the 21st through the 24th, with the hardest hit areas mainly along and north of Interstate 80.  Reported rainfall was as high as 4 inches (Cedar Rapids) during this period, while some locations received 5 to 6 inches.   The high amounts of water from smaller creeks and streams led to rapid rises on the area's larger rivers and streams, then major to near record flooding.  Most of the hardest hit counties, flood-wise, were along the U.S. Highway 20 corridor in Iowa.  In Manchester, Iowa, the Maquoketa River reached its second highest level ever, second only to a crest in the 1950s.  Flooding closed the major east-west road through the city.  That road is also a state highway.  The high water also forced evacuations of some businesses.  Some homes were affected, too.Independence, Iowa also encountered major flooding on the Wapsipinicon River.  Its crest was the sixth highest on record.  Many homes were affected, and the high water forced the evacuation of some businesses in town just like in Manchester.  In Independence, some normally small creeks became major waterways during and after the heavy rain, which flooded some houses and businesses that were some distance from those houses that were affected by high water on the Wapsipinicon River.  High water forced the closing of Iowa Highway 150 on the south side of town, where the road crosses the river.  With this major road shut down, access to the city was inconvenient from the south.  It required one to either travel several miles east on U.S. Highway 20, then back the same several miles to Independence, or to travel west a little and then take a road into the west side of Independence.Jones County, Iowa, also experienced problems from high water on the Wapsipinicon River.  The river in Anamosa crested at the second highest level on record.  The flood fight in Anamosa was successful in keeping most of the city safe from flooding.The second major rain event of the month occurred from the 29th through the 31st.  Reported rainfall was as much as two and a half inches of rain with other locations reporting as much as 3 to 4 inches.  This additional rain led to additional rises and crests on some rivers, with most of the crests occurring in June.  The second crests were in some cases the same as or higher than the first crests.  Lower sections of the Wapsipinicon River, for example, in Clinton and Scott counties, experienced high second crests.  Large amounts of water coming downstream from the first heavy rain event combined with runoff from the second rain event to produce the second highest crest on record on the Wapsipinicon River near De Witt, Iowa.  The high water forced the closing of Old U.S. Highway 61 south of De Witt, Iowa, along with the closing of a business along the river by the highway.  The present U.S. Highway 61-a vital link between northern Scott County, Iowa, and Clinton County, Iowa-was unaffected.The Rock, Pecatonica, and La Moine rivers in Illinois also experienced flooding due to the heavy rains.  Minor flooding occurred on the Rock River while moderate flooding occurred on the Pecatonica River.  The La Moine River experienced minor flooding.The large amounts of water from the tributary rivers in Iowa and Illinois led to rises on the Mississippi River.  Although the entire river rose in response to the large amounts of water, the river rose above flood stage from Lock and Dam15 in the Quad Cities to Gregory Landing, Missouri.  Most of the rest of the crests occurred in June.  The Mississippi River in the Quad Cities did crest during May, however, and it crested just over flood stage.  Only minor flooding resulted.

In summary, a significant round of severe thunderstorms affected parts of west Texas during the afternoon and evening of the 11th. At least two supercell storms produced giant hail and one strong tornado over the region.A supercell thunderstorm tracked across Terrell County in the west Texas Lower Trans Pecos region during the late afternoon hours. Multiple reports of large hail including two different instances of tennis ball sized stones were received as this storm tracked east along U.S. Highway 90 between Sanderson and Dryden.A second area of convection erupted over the eastern Permian Basin by late afternoon and continued into the evening hours. A severe storm associated with this activity produced half-dollar size hail in the Westbrook community. An isolated classic supercell evolved from this complex of storms and took on a distinctly deviant southeastward storm motion. This storm took on radar characteristics consistent with a classic tornadic supercell. Hail up to the size of golfballs was observed southeast of Colorado City as the storm evolved into its tornadic phase. A long-lived significant tornado tracked across mainly rural areas of Mitchell County just after sunset. The tornado resulted in three injuries when it crossed State Route 208 and blew a vehicle off of the highway. Severe rear flank downdraft winds also resulted in widespread wind damage south of the tornado's path.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A second severe thunderstorm developed near Westbrook and resulted in numerous reports of large hail up to the size of golfballs along a broad swath from the city of Westbrook to along State Route 208 south of Colorado City. This storm evolved into a right moving classic supercell as it tracked southeast across the central parts of Mitchell County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low level jet moving over a warm front from Northern Missouri into Central Illinois combined with an upper level disturbance to produce thunderstorms across Iowa and Northern Illinois.  As the storms became better organized, they were prolific producers of hail from 0.75 to 1 inch.  In Muscatine County Iowa, the storms organized into a small bow echo that moved through Rock Island, Henry, Bureau, and Putnam counties in Illinois.  Southern Henry County Illinois took the brunt of the bow echo with near continuous damage from Interstate 74 to Galva, Illinois with the worst damage in Galva.	A second round of thunderstorms developed around dawn from boundaries left over from the overnight storms.  Due to a drier atmosphere, the hail produced by this round of storms was much larger.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms rumbled across south-central Nebraska during the late afternoon and evening hours.  These storms produced hail, strong winds and a few tornadoes.  The storms started out in Gosper county and moved northeast.  There were several reports of funnel clouds in eastern Gosper county.  As the storms continued into Dawson and Buffalo counties, storm chasers continued to report funnels and hail.  The first tornado set down in southeast Sherman county near Rockville and was observed for a few minutes.  The next twister was in southwest Howard county near Farwell.  Another tornado was reported by a sheriff's deputy near the junction of Nebraska highways 92 and 11.  These tornadoes were in open county and caused little in the way of damage.  The town of Elba in Howard county has pummeled by large hail for period of time.  Broken windows and trees stripped of leaves were common throughout the small community.  The most destructive tornado occurred near the village of Cushing.  The tornado set down on a farm west of town and damaged several outbuildings and threw irrigation pipe across a field.  The tornado then cut a path across the south end of town, again damaging several outbuildings and some minor damage to a home.  The tornado dissipated just southeast of town.  Other storms south of these produced strong winds from Grand Island to near Hebron.  Trees and power poles were damaged from the strong winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Flooding of the Ohio River continued from late May into early June. At J.T. Myers Lock and Dam near Uniontown, the river crested at 42.3 feet on June 6. This was several feet over the 37-foot flood stage. Flooding of low-lying areas and bottomlands near the river occurred. Several thousand acres of cropland were inundated, mainly in Henderson County. Since crops were planted, some farmers experienced major losses. Crop damage estimates are contained in the May Storm Data report. A few roads near the river were flooded, mainly secondary access roads.

Minor to moderate flooding of the Ohio River continued from late May into early June. The river crested above flood stage at all gage points on the Illinois side. Crests were only about a foot or two above flood stage at Brookport and Golconda. At Grand Chain and Cairo, the river crested 3 to 5 feet above flood stage. Flood stage at Grand Chain is 42 feet, and at Cairo flood stage is 40 feet. The crest at Shawneetown was 42.1 feet, well above the 33-foot flood stage. Flooding of bottomlands and low-lying fields near the river was considerable in some areas. A few river access roads were flooded, and some riverside parks were partially inundated.

The combination of spring tides caused by the full moon and a residual onshore flow caused by a departing low pressure system caused minor tidal flooding during the late afternoon and early evening high tide cycle along coastal New Jersey. The high tide reached 6.9 feet above mean lower low water at Sandy Hook (Monmouth County) and 6.8 feet above mean lower low water in Cape May (Cape May County). Minor tidal flooding usually starts at 6.7 feet above mean lower low water. The low pressure system which caused the onshore flow formed along a warm frontal boundary on the Delmarva Peninsula during the evening of May 31st and moved slowly northeast on June 1st. The low pressure system passed closed to Nantucket, Massachusetts during the afternoon of June 1st.

A tropical airmass was in place over Iowa as a weak cold front moved southeast into the state.  At the same time, a tropical feature lifted north across Texas into Oklahoma and fed moisture into the state.  Dew points south of the front rose into the mid 70s by the late morning hours.  Precipitable water values were in the one and one half to two inch range with CAPE values across the state ranging from 1500 J/kg along the front to 3500 J/kg a ways ahead of the front.  Zero to 3 km CAPE values were between 100 and 175 J/kg.  During the mid morning hours thunderstorms fired up in northwest Iowa as the MCV from the previous nights MCS moved northeast into western Iowa.  The thunderstorms expanded through the morning into the afternoon hours.  Most of the storms were tropical in nature, but did produce pea to marble size hail at many locations.  There were a few reports of hail up to an inch in diameter.  As the event unfolded, a few of the storms produced downburst winds.  Wind gusts were limited to around 60 MPH.  Two barns were blown down in Webster County by the high winds.  The main event was the heavy tropical rainfall.  A band of heavy rainfall extended from west central into north central Iowa.  A band of two to four inch rainfall extended from near Sac City toward Fort Dodge into the Mason City area.  Locally heavier amounts of 4 to 5 inches were received.  Numerous roads were flooded in Webster County with a main bridge into Fort Dodge close due to high water.  Fifteen roads were flooded in Cerro Gordo County.  In Calhoun County, U.S. Highway 20 east of Rockwell City was under water with numerous county roads flooded.  Heavy rainfall in Des Moines caused flash flooding with water flowing over 2 feet deep over U.S. Highway 6 in town.  Nearly two inches of rain fell within a 30 minute period in the area to produce the flash flood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The front that moved through our area on Wednesday June 9th maintained its identity and began to move north as a warm front during the afternoon of the 13th. The first cell of the day became a long-lived supercell. This storm moved through the Midland and Bay City areas, over the south end of Saginaw Bay, and into Huron county before moving out over the open waters of Lake Huron. Later in the afternoon and during the evening a nearly solid line of storms developed along a north-south surface trough over western lower Michigan. These storms developed bowing characteristics as they moved into southeast Michigan and generated some straight-line wind damage. The Midland Fire Department called out two extra crews to answer about 30 storm-related calls of downed wires, broken utility poles and fallen trees. At least two trees crashed into homes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained weather spotter estimated a 58 mph thunderstorm wind gust.

For the second time in a week, severe thunderstorm winds impacted the Cibola Ranch north of Shafter. Employees at the ranch reported that large tree limbs were broken by 70 MPH winds on the evening of the 7th as an isolated severe thunderstorm moved south across parts of Presidio County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moist and unstable air along a stalled frontal boundary set the stage for supercell thunderstorm development during the afternoon and evening hours.  This was round number two for the day.  Numerous supercells developed across southern Wisconsin by the late afternoon hours, which produced three tornadoes, numerous funnel clouds, several large hail reports, and heavy rains.  Funnel cloud reports were collected from Columbia, Dane, Rock, Dodge, and Waukesha counties between 1720 CST and 1913 CST.  The first tornado spun up 3.3 miles east-southeast of Stoughton (Dane Co.), the second tornado spun up 1.2 miles southeast of De Forest (Dane Co.), and the third tornado spun up 2 miles southwest of Fall River (Columbia Co.).  All three tornadoes had no damage associated with them and were all classified as F0s (for detailed path lengths, path widths, and spin up and dissipating points, please consult details above).  In addition to tornadoes, funnel clouds, and large hail, these storms produced heavy rain.  Urban flooding resulted across Ozaukee County after storms produced 1.25 inches of rain in only a 30 minute period.  A few roads were closed and gravel washouts were common.  Refer to several flood and flash flood events for May 23rd, 24th, and 25th, for related information.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: An isolated supercell thunderstorm propagated south across Terrell County during the late afternoon of the 9th. The storm generally affected rural areas of the county, but a local rancher reported three quarter inch hail northwest of Dryden.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very unstable situation took shape over Iowa during the day on the 11th.  A nearly stationary frontal boundary extended nearly east to west across the state along U.S. Highway 20, or roughly from Fort Dodge to Waterloo.  Very unstable air was to the south of the front with dew point temperatures in the low to mid 70s common.  By early afternoon, CAPE values were near 5000 J/KG with lifted indices in the -10 to -12 C. range.  A dry line advanced east toward the state along with the passage of a short wave lifting northeast across the area.  Thunderstorms fired along the triple point by the early afternoon hours in northwest Iowa.  The storms became severe very quickly and produced tornadoes as the sounding profile became very favorable.  In addition, significant mid level cooling took place as 700 mb temperatures fell several degrees during the day.   Most of the storms remained over the north third of the state with numerous reports of tornadoes.  The bulk of the tornadoes progressed southeast from northwest Iowa into the central counties of the state as the afternoon turned into evening.  For the most part, the tornadoes were quite small with only a few remaining on the ground for more than a few tenths of a mile.  Two tornadoes in Palo Alto and Emmet Counties were on the ground for a significant period of time, however they tracked over open country.  There were several tornadoes in Webster County.  Most of them were also small and did little damage, however one tornado near Otho hit two farmsteads there causing considerable damage.  One farmstead was nearly destroyed, including significant damage to the house.  Hail was common with the storms with much of it in the three quarter to one and one quarter inch diameter range.  There were a few golf ball size hail reports in Webster and Hamilton Counties, and one tennis ball size hail report in Stratford in Hamilton County.  Spotty reports of high were were received.  Winds were in the 60 to 70 MPH range.  Rainfall became a problem in a couple areas.  In Kossuth County rainfall of 2 to over 3 inches fell in under 2 hours causing flooding around the County.  Several roads became flooded, including Iowa Highway 9 and U.S. Highway 169.  Very heavy rain in the 2 to 4 inch range fell in Hamilton County during a 2 hour period.  This caused considerable flooding in the county, especially over the northwest half.  There was one high wind event.  In what turned out to be a high wind event occurred in Marion County.  A 60 MPH wind was recorded in Pella.  The event was in the wake of the line of thunderstorms and actually effected a several county area with winds of 40 to 50 MPH.  Temperatures shot up 9 degrees in a few minutes at the Des Moines Airport as a 51 MPH wind gust pushed the temperature up to 90 during the mid evening hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active and very complicated round of severe thunderstorms affected west Texas during the late afternoon and evening of the 5th. Severe weather development was focused in two areas of the region. Convective initiation occurred first near a sub-synoptic scale outflow boundary that was situated across the southeast Permian Basin. This feature was a remnant from overnight convection to the northeast of the area. Two supercell thunderstorms developed along the boundary over rural areas of southeast Midland and northern Upton Counties. As these storms moved east, storm-scale outflow boundaries were observed in local warning radar base reflectivity and velocity data arcing away from the storms toward the west. Both of these boundaries interacted with the larger scale baroclinic boundary under a field of strongly growing convective towers over southern and central Midland County and northeast Crane County. A series of at least four landspout tornadoes were observed as these interactions occurred.The mesoscale boundary began propagating west-northwest across the basin as the supercell storms provided convective enhancement to the cool (east) side of the boundary. Meanwhile strong to severe thunderstorms began propagating east from the mountainous areas of southeast New Mexico and southwest Texas. The convectively enhanced outflow boundary interacted with the complex of storms over the Upper Trans Pecos region. Large hail and two tornadoes were observed in east-central Reeves County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active and very complicated round of severe thunderstorms affected west Texas during the late afternoon and evening of the 5th. Severe weather development was focused in two areas of the region. Convective initiation occurred first near a sub-synoptic scale outflow boundary that was situated across the southeast Permian Basin. This feature was a remnant from overnight convection to the northeast of the area. Two supercell thunderstorms developed along the boundary over rural areas of southeast Midland and northern Upton Counties. As these storms moved east, storm-scale outflow boundaries were observed in local warning radar base reflectivity and velocity data arcing away from the storms toward the west. Both of these boundaries interacted with the larger scale baroclinic boundary under a field of strongly growing convective towers over southern and central Midland County and northeast Crane County. A series of at least four landspout tornadoes were observed as these interactions occurred.The mesoscale boundary began propagating west-northwest across the basin as the supercell storms provided convective enhancement to the cool (east) side of the boundary. Meanwhile strong to severe thunderstorms began propagating east from the mountainous areas of southeast New Mexico and southwest Texas. The convectively enhanced outflow boundary interacted with the complex of storms over the Upper Trans Pecos region. Large hail and two tornadoes were observed in east-central Reeves County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Odessa Police Department reported a tornado (landspout) in northeast Crane County near U.S. Highway 385.A series of at least four landspout tornadoes developed as outflow from two isolated severe thunderstorms interacted with a pre-existing boundary remnant from the previous night's convection. Strong towering cumulus clouds above the boundary interactions provided sufficient vertical stretching to result in narrow dust filled vortices that visually extended toward the cloud bases. These landspouts were observed by many people in Midland and law officials in Odessa resulting in numerous reports from both public and local emergency officials.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tropical airmass was in place over Iowa as a weak cold front moved southeast into the state.  At the same time, a tropical feature lifted north across Texas into Oklahoma and fed moisture into the state.  Dew points south of the front rose into the mid 70s by the late morning hours.  Precipitable water values were in the one and one half to two inch range with CAPE values across the state ranging from 1500 J/kg along the front to 3500 J/kg a ways ahead of the front.  Zero to 3 km CAPE values were between 100 and 175 J/kg.  During the mid morning hours thunderstorms fired up in northwest Iowa as the MCV from the previous nights MCS moved northeast into western Iowa.  The thunderstorms expanded through the morning into the afternoon hours.  Most of the storms were tropical in nature, but did produce pea to marble size hail at many locations.  There were a few reports of hail up to an inch in diameter.  As the event unfolded, a few of the storms produced downburst winds.  Wind gusts were limited to around 60 MPH.  Two barns were blown down in Webster County by the high winds.  The main event was the heavy tropical rainfall.  A band of heavy rainfall extended from west central into north central Iowa.  A band of two to four inch rainfall extended from near Sac City toward Fort Dodge into the Mason City area.  Locally heavier amounts of 4 to 5 inches were received.  Numerous roads were flooded in Webster County with a main bridge into Fort Dodge close due to high water.  Fifteen roads were flooded in Cerro Gordo County.  In Calhoun County, U.S. Highway 20 east of Rockwell City was under water with numerous county roads flooded.  Heavy rainfall in Des Moines caused flash flooding with water flowing over 2 feet deep over U.S. Highway 6 in town.  Nearly two inches of rain fell within a 30 minute period in the area to produce the flash flood.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 30th, a warm front was draped across eastern Kentucky.  With extremely moist and unstable air, this boundary helped spark the beginning of a most unusual event for eastern Kentucky, and for that matter, for the country.  Countless supercell thunderstorms developed along this boundary for hours on end, causing widespread tree damage and damage to structures.  Flash flooding was also occurring with these storms which contained torrential rain.  Unfortunately for eastern Kentucky, this was not the end to the severe weather or the flooding.  Later in the night, mostly in the early hours of May 31st, a potent cold front burst through, bringing destruction to most if not all eastern Kentucky counties.  Also, so much rain had fallen from the previous afternoon and evening, coupled with more heavy rain during the morning of May 31st, that widespread aerial flooding occurred.  For some counties, as was the case for Estill and Powell Counties, the aerial flooding lasted for days.  The cost of these storms totaled easily in the millions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In summary, a significant round of severe thunderstorms affected parts of west Texas during the afternoon and evening of the 11th. At least two supercell storms produced giant hail and one strong tornado over the region.A supercell thunderstorm tracked across Terrell County in the west Texas Lower Trans Pecos region during the late afternoon hours. Multiple reports of large hail including two different instances of tennis ball sized stones were received as this storm tracked east along U.S. Highway 90 between Sanderson and Dryden.A second area of convection erupted over the eastern Permian Basin by late afternoon and continued into the evening hours. A severe storm associated with this activity produced half-dollar size hail in the Westbrook community. An isolated classic supercell evolved from this complex of storms and took on a distinctly deviant southeastward storm motion. This storm took on radar characteristics consistent with a classic tornadic supercell. Hail up to the size of golfballs was observed southeast of Colorado City as the storm evolved into its tornadic phase. A long-lived significant tornado tracked across mainly rural areas of Mitchell County just after sunset. The tornado resulted in three injuries when it crossed State Route 208 and blew a vehicle off of the highway. Severe rear flank downdraft winds also resulted in widespread wind damage south of the tornado's path.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service damage survey team concluded that a significant tornado struck rural areas of southeastern Mitchell County during the evening of the 11th. The team examined a damage path marked by shredded vegetation (mostly mesquite trees),  downed utility poles, agricultural fences, and a complex of destroyed mobile homes that extended over ten miles in a continuous horseshoe shaped path that crossed State Route 208 twenty miles south-southeast of Colorado City.The tornado developed seventeen miles south-southeast of Colorado City around 2028 CST. Damage indicates the tornado's motion was initially toward the southeast then east as it crossed the heavily traveled State Route 208. Two Texas Tech University students traveling north on 208 (south of the tornado's path) watched as a Ford Expedition drove into the tornadic circulation. The large sports utility vehicle was blown 100 yards off of the highway. Evidence supports the vehicle was rolled a considerable distance by the tornadic winds, but it is unclear whether it became airborne. Three motorists were transferred to local hospitals. One person sustained serious injuries that included a broken back.A detailed damage path analysis and corresponding radar data suggest that the tornado then tracked very slowly east a few miles before curving to the northeast. Similar curved damage paths (turning left of the tornado's original motion) are commonly observed when well-developed tornadoes enter the dissipation stage. The tornado proved to remain very dangerous, however, as eight mobile homes were destroyed by the tornado near the end of its life cycle twenty miles southeast of Colorado City. The light weight and unanchored structures were blown over and shredded by the dissipation stage tornadic winds. The trailers were arranged in a complex and were used to provide shelter for groups of hunters that frequent the ranch property. They were not occupied when the tornado struck.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active and very complicated round of severe thunderstorms affected west Texas during the late afternoon and evening of the 5th. As these storms moved east, storm-scale outflow boundaries were observed in local warning radar base reflectivity and velocity data arcing away from the storms toward the west. Both of these boundaries interacted with the larger scale baroclinic boundary under a field of strongly growing convective towers over southern and central Midland County and northeast Crane County. A series of at least four landspout tornadoes were observed as these interactions occurred.The mesoscale boundary began propagating west-northwest across the basin as the supercell storms provided convective enhancement to the cool (east) side of the boundary. Meanwhile strong to severe thunderstorms began propagating east from the mountainous areas of southeast New Mexico and southwest Texas. The convectively enhanced outflow boundary interacted with the complex of storms over the Upper Trans Pecos region. Large hail and two tornadoes were observed in east-central Reeves County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 30th, a warm front was draped across eastern Kentucky.  With extremely moist and unstable air, this boundary helped spark the beginning of a most unusual event for eastern Kentucky, and for that matter, for the country.  Countless supercell thunderstorms developed along this boundary for hours on end, causing widespread tree damage and damage to structures.  Flash flooding was also occurring with these storms which contained torrential rain.  Unfortunately for eastern Kentucky, this was not the end to the severe weather or the flooding.  Later in the night, mostly in the early hours of May 31st, a potent cold front burst through, bringing destruction to most if not all eastern Kentucky counties.  Also, so much rain had fallen from the previous afternoon and evening, coupled with more heavy rain during the morning of May 31st, that widespread aerial flooding occurred.  For some counties, as was the case for Estill and Powell Counties, the aerial flooding lasted for days.  The cost of these storms totaled easily in the millions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A very unstable situation took shape over Iowa during the day on the 11th.  A nearly stationary frontal boundary extended nearly east to west across the state along U.S. Highway 20, or roughly from Fort Dodge to Waterloo.  Very unstable air was to the south of the front with dew point temperatures in the low to mid 70s common.  By early afternoon, CAPE values were near 5000 J/KG with lifted indices in the -10 to -12 C. range.  A dry line advanced east toward the state along with the passage of a short wave lifting northeast across the area.  Thunderstorms fired along the triple point by the early afternoon hours in northwest Iowa.  The storms became severe very quickly and produced tornadoes as the sounding profile became very favorable.  In addition, significant mid level cooling took place as 700 mb temperatures fell several degrees during the day.   Most of the storms remained over the north third of the state with numerous reports of tornadoes.  The bulk of the tornadoes progressed southeast from northwest Iowa into the central counties of the state as the afternoon turned into evening.  For the most part, the tornadoes were quite small with only a few remaining on the ground for more than a few tenths of a mile.  Two tornadoes in Palo Alto and Emmet Counties were on the ground for a significant period of time, however they tracked over open country.  There were several tornadoes in Webster County.  Most of them were also small and did little damage, however one tornado near Otho hit two farmsteads there causing considerable damage.  One farmstead was nearly destroyed, including significant damage to the house.  Hail was common with the storms with much of it in the three quarter to one and one quarter inch diameter range.  There were a few golf ball size hail reports in Webster and Hamilton Counties, and one tennis ball size hail report in Stratford in Hamilton County.  Spotty reports of high were were received.  Winds were in the 60 to 70 MPH range.  Rainfall became a problem in a couple areas.  In Kossuth County rainfall of 2 to over 3 inches fell in under 2 hours causing flooding around the County.  Several roads became flooded, including Iowa Highway 9 and U.S. Highway 169.  Very heavy rain in the 2 to 4 inch range fell in Hamilton County during a 2 hour period.  This caused considerable flooding in the county, especially over the northwest half.  There was one high wind event.  In what turned out to be a high wind event occurred in Marion County.  A 60 MPH wind was recorded in Pella.  The event was in the wake of the line of thunderstorms and actually effected a several county area with winds of 40 to 50 MPH.  Temperatures shot up 9 degrees in a few minutes at the Des Moines Airport as a 51 MPH wind gust pushed the temperature up to 90 during the mid evening hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The most significant heavy rainfall and flooding event of June occurred on June 19-24. During this period thunderstorms developed in the Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles and then moved through the western half of Oklahoma on three consecutive days on June 19-22. These storms also produced severe hail and wind gusts on June 21.Rainfall totals for the 72-hour period ending at 7:00 am CDT on June 22 reached 2 to 3 inches in a wide swath that included most of northwest, west central, north central, and central Oklahoma. Hardest hit was the Cimarron River basin in northern Oklahoma where storm total precipitation amounts of 5 to 6+ inches were observed in parts of Harper, Woods, Woodward, Major, Blaine, Kingfisher, and Logan counties. The subsequent heavy runoff produced by these rains generated flash flooding and riverine flooding in northwestern and central Oklahoma.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Three inch diameter tree limbs were downed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moist and unstable air along a stalled frontal boundary set the stage for supercell thunderstorm development during the afternoon and evening hours.  This was round number two for the day.  Numerous supercells developed across southern Wisconsin by the late afternoon hours, which produced three tornadoes, numerous funnel clouds, several large hail reports, and heavy rains.  Funnel cloud reports were collected from Columbia, Dane, Rock, Dodge, and Waukesha counties between 1720 CST and 1913 CST.  The first tornado spun up 3.3 miles east-southeast of Stoughton (Dane Co.), the second tornado spun up 1.2 miles southeast of De Forest (Dane Co.), and the third tornado spun up 2 miles southwest of Fall River (Columbia Co.).  All three tornadoes had no damage associated with them and were all classified as F0s (for detailed path lengths, path widths, and spin up and dissipating points, please consult details above).  In addition to tornadoes, funnel clouds, and large hail, these storms produced heavy rain.  Urban flooding resulted across Ozaukee County after storms produced 1.25 inches of rain in only a 30 minute period.  A few roads were closed and gravel washouts were common.  Refer to several flood and flash flood events for May 23rd, 24th, and 25th, for related information.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unstable airmass was over Iowa during the afternoon ahead of a very slow moving cold front.  The cold front was located northeast to southwest over the far northwest corner of the state.  Dew point temperatures rose into the low to mid 70s with actual temperatures in the mid to upper 80s ahead of the front.  The sheer environment was very weak with less than 20 kts of sheer in both the zero to 3 km and zero to 6 km layer.  A few thunderstorms developed along the cold front during the late afternoon hours.  The storms became better organized during the early evening and produced severe weather over northwest and north central Iowa.  Hail up to the size of nickels fell in those areas. Dew point temperatures rose into the low to mid 70s with actual temperatures in the mid to upper 80s ahead of the front.  The sheer environment was very weak with less than 20 kts of sheer in both the zero to 3 km and zero to 6 km layer.  A few thunderstorms developed along the cold front during the late afternoon hours.  The storms became better organized during the early evening and produced severe weather over northwest and north central Iowa.  Hail up to the size of nickels fell in those areas.  One of the storms produced high winds in Worth County, downing trees and damaging outbuildings and an LP tank east of Northwood.

A very unstable situation took shape over Iowa during the day on the 11th.  A nearly stationary frontal boundary extended nearly east to west across the state along U.S. Highway 20, or roughly from Fort Dodge to Waterloo.  Very unstable air was to the south of the front with dew point temperatures in the low to mid 70s common.  By early afternoon, CAPE values were near 5000 J/KG with lifted indices in the -10 to -12 C. range.  A dry line advanced east toward the state along with the passage of a short wave lifting northeast across the area.  Thunderstorms fired along the triple point by the early afternoon hours in northwest Iowa.  The storms became severe very quickly and produced tornadoes as the sounding profile became very favorable.  In addition, significant mid level cooling took place as 700 mb temperatures fell several degrees during the day.   Most of the storms remained over the north third of the state with numerous reports of tornadoes.  The bulk of the tornadoes progressed southeast from northwest Iowa into the central counties of the state as the afternoon turned into evening.  For the most part, the tornadoes were quite small with only a few remaining on the ground for more than a few tenths of a mile.  Two tornadoes in Palo Alto and Emmet Counties were on the ground for a significant period of time, however they tracked over open country.  There were several tornadoes in Webster County.  Most of them were also small and did little damage, however one tornado near Otho hit two farmsteads there causing considerable damage.  One farmstead was nearly destroyed, including significant damage to the house.  Hail was common with the storms with much of it in the three quarter to one and one quarter inch diameter range.  There were a few golf ball size hail reports in Webster and Hamilton Counties, and one tennis ball size hail report in Stratford in Hamilton County.  Spotty reports of high were were received.  Winds were in the 60 to 70 MPH range.  Rainfall became a problem in a couple areas.  In Kossuth County rainfall of 2 to over 3 inches fell in under 2 hours causing flooding around the County.  Several roads became flooded, including Iowa Highway 9 and U.S. Highway 169.  Very heavy rain in the 2 to 4 inch range fell in Hamilton County during a 2 hour period.  This caused considerable flooding in the county, especially over the northwest half.  There was one high wind event.  In what turned out to be a high wind event occurred in Marion County.  A 60 MPH wind was recorded in Pella.  The event was in the wake of the line of thunderstorms and actually effected a several county area with winds of 40 to 50 MPH.  Temperatures shot up 9 degrees in a few minutes at the Des Moines Airport as a 51 MPH wind gust pushed the temperature up to 90 during the mid evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tornado tracked through mostly open area with only minor damage reported.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 100 year-old bank building in Toyah was destroyed when strong winds affected the community on the evening of the 17th. Radar reflectivity data depicted strong to severe thunderstorms well to the west of Toyah in adjacent Culberson County, however, only light reflectivity returns were indicated in the Toyah area and appeared to be associated with anvil blow-off down wind of the severe storms. The Reeves County Emergency Manager reported winds around 50 MPH when the building was destroyed. These winds were likely associated with outflow from the distant storms. The structural integrity of the historic building may have been compromised by the extensive flooding event which affected the community in early April.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The front that moved through our area on Wednesday June 9th maintained its identity and began to move north as a warm front during the afternoon of the 13th. The first cell of the day became a long-lived supercell. This storm moved through the Midland and Bay City areas, over the south end of Saginaw Bay, and into Huron county before moving out over the open waters of Lake Huron. Later in the afternoon and during the evening a nearly solid line of storms developed along a north-south surface trough over western lower Michigan. These storms developed bowing characteristics as they moved into southeast Michigan and generated some straight-line wind damage. The Midland Fire Department called out two extra crews to answer about 30 storm-related calls of downed wires, broken utility poles and fallen trees. At least two trees crashed into homes.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A trained weather spotter reported 5 inch diameter tree limbs blown down.
A trailer and a barn were destroyed. One house was damaged. Several trees were blown down.
A large tree and some power lines were blown down.
Thunderstorm wind gusts estimated at over 60 mph downed large trees that blocked several city streets.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active and very complicated round of severe thunderstorms affected west Texas during the late afternoon and evening of the 5th. Severe weather development was focused in two areas of the region. Convective initiation occurred first near a sub-synoptic scale outflow boundary that was situated across the southeast Permian Basin. This feature was a remnant from overnight convection to the northeast of the area. Two supercell thunderstorms developed along the boundary over rural areas of southeast Midland and northern Upton Counties. As these storms moved east, storm-scale outflow boundaries were observed in local warning radar base reflectivity and velocity data arcing away from the storms toward the west. Both of these boundaries interacted with the larger scale baroclinic boundary under a field of strongly growing convective towers over southern and central Midland County and northeast Crane County. A series of at least four landspout tornadoes were observed as these interactions occurred.The mesoscale boundary began propagating west-northwest across the basin as the supercell storms provided convective enhancement to the cool (east) side of the boundary. Meanwhile strong to severe thunderstorms began propagating east from the mountainous areas of southeast New Mexico and southwest Texas. The convectively enhanced outflow boundary interacted with the complex of storms over the Upper Trans Pecos region. Large hail and two tornadoes were observed in east-central Reeves County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The first in a series of landspout tornadoes developed just west of State Highway 349 south of Midland.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated severe thunderstorms popped up and produced large hail. This day would be the first of 6 or 7 consecutive days with thunderstorms and possible severe weather across south-central and southeast Wisconsin due to a stangant weather pattern that allowed several cold fronts to stall over Illinois and then move north as a warm front the next day.

A supercell thunderstorm developed over Ward County, and propagated northeast along and just north of Interstate 20. This storm produced golfball size hail near Monahans. Continuous nickel to quarter size hail was reported by law enforcement officials from Monahans Sandhills State Park northeast along Interstate 20 across extreme northwest Crane County and into southwest Ector County near mile marker 92. Numerous reports of nickel to quarter size hail also accompanied the storm from West Odessa to the Gardendale Community in northeast Ector County. Hailstones the size of tennis balls reportedly fell in Gardendale, but reports of damage were minimal. The storm continued to produce large hail to the size of nickels as it moved across northwest Midland County.

On the afternoon of May 30th, a warm front was draped across eastern Kentucky.  With extremely moist and unstable air, this boundary helped spark the beginning of a most unusual event for eastern Kentucky, and for that matter, for the country.  Countless supercell thunderstorms developed along this boundary for hours on end, causing widespread tree damage and damage to structures.  Flash flooding was also occurring with these storms which contained torrential rain.  Unfortunately for eastern Kentucky, this was not the end to the severe weather or the flooding.  Later in the night, mostly in the early hours of May 31st, a potent cold front burst through, bringing destruction to most if not all eastern Kentucky counties.  Also, so much rain had fallen from the previous afternoon and evening, coupled with more heavy rain during the morning of May 31st, that widespread aerial flooding occurred.  For some counties, as was the case for Estill and Powell Counties, the aerial flooding lasted for days.  The cost of these storms totaled easily in the millions.

Severe thunderstorms rumbled across south-central Nebraska during the late afternoon and evening hours.  These storms produced hail, strong winds and a few tornadoes.  The storms started out in Gosper county and moved northeast.  There were several reports of funnel clouds in eastern Gosper county.  As the storms continued into Dawson and Buffalo counties, storm chasers continued to report funnels and hail.  The first tornado set down in southeast Sherman county near Rockville and was observed for a few minutes.  The next twister was in southwest Howard county near Farwell.  Another tornado was reported by a sheriff's deputy near the junction of Nebraska highways 92 and 11.  These tornadoes were in open county and caused little in the way of damage.  The town of Elba in Howard county has pummeled by large hail for period of time.  Broken windows and trees stripped of leaves were common throughout the small community.  The most destructive tornado occurred near the village of Cushing.  The tornado set down on a farm west of town and damaged several outbuildings and threw irrigation pipe across a field.  The tornado then cut a path across the south end of town, again damaging several outbuildings and some minor damage to a home.  The tornado dissipated just southeast of town.  Other storms south of these produced strong winds from Grand Island to near Hebron.  Trees and power poles were damaged from the strong winds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 30th, a warm front was draped across eastern Kentucky.  With extremely moist and unstable air, this boundary helped spark the beginning of a most unusual event for eastern Kentucky, and for that matter, for the country.  Countless supercell thunderstorms developed along this boundary for hours on end, causing widespread tree damage and damage to structures.  Flash flooding was also occurring with these storms which contained torrential rain.  Unfortunately for eastern Kentucky, this was not the end to the severe weather or the flooding.  Later in the night, mostly in the early hours of May 31st, a potent cold front burst through, bringing destruction to most if not all eastern Kentucky counties.  Also, so much rain had fallen from the previous afternoon and evening, coupled with more heavy rain during the morning of May 31st, that widespread aerial flooding occurred.  For some counties, as was the case for Estill and Powell Counties, the aerial flooding lasted for days.  The cost of these storms totaled easily in the millions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An active and very complicated round of severe thunderstorms affected west Texas during the late afternoon and evening of the 5th. Severe weather development was focused in two areas of the region. Convective initiation occurred first near a sub-synoptic scale outflow boundary that was situated across the southeast Permian Basin. This feature was a remnant from overnight convection to the northeast of the area. Two supercell thunderstorms developed along the boundary over rural areas of southeast Midland and northern Upton Counties. As these storms moved east, storm-scale outflow boundaries were observed in local warning radar base reflectivity and velocity data arcing away from the storms toward the west. Both of these boundaries interacted with the larger scale baroclinic boundary under a field of strongly growing convective towers over southern and central Midland County and northeast Crane County. A series of at least four landspout tornadoes were observed as these interactions occurred.The mesoscale boundary began propagating west-northwest across the basin as the supercell storms provided convective enhancement to the cool (east) side of the boundary. Meanwhile strong to severe thunderstorms began propagating east from the mountainous areas of southeast New Mexico and southwest Texas. The convectively enhanced outflow boundary interacted with the complex of storms over the Upper Trans Pecos region. Large hail and two tornadoes were observed in east-central Reeves County.

In another wind incident, a semi-tractortrailer was blown over on Interstate 35 about 3 miles south of Clear Lake.

A very unstable situation took shape over Iowa during the day on the 11th.  A nearly stationary frontal boundary extended nearly east to west across the state along U.S. Highway 20, or roughly from Fort Dodge to Waterloo.  Very unstable air was to the south of the front with dew point temperatures in the low to mid 70s common.  By early afternoon, CAPE values were near 5000 J/KG with lifted indices in the -10 to -12 C. range.  A dry line advanced east toward the state along with the passage of a short wave lifting northeast across the area.  Thunderstorms fired along the triple point by the early afternoon hours in northwest Iowa.  The storms became severe very quickly and produced tornadoes as the sounding profile became very favorable.  In addition, significant mid level cooling took place as 700 mb temperatures fell several degrees during the day.   Most of the storms remained over the north third of the state with numerous reports of tornadoes.  The bulk of the tornadoes progressed southeast from northwest Iowa into the central counties of the state as the afternoon turned into evening.  For the most part, the tornadoes were quite small with only a few remaining on the ground for more than a few tenths of a mile.  Two tornadoes in Palo Alto and Emmet Counties were on the ground for a significant period of time, however they tracked over open country.  There were several tornadoes in Webster County.  Most of them were also small and did little damage, however one tornado near Otho hit two farmsteads there causing considerable damage.  One farmstead was nearly destroyed, including significant damage to the house.  Hail was common with the storms with much of it in the three quarter to one and one quarter inch diameter range.  There were a few golf ball size hail reports in Webster and Hamilton Counties, and one tennis ball size hail report in Stratford in Hamilton County.  Spotty reports of high were were received.  Winds were in the 60 to 70 MPH range.  Rainfall became a problem in a couple areas.  In Kossuth County rainfall of 2 to over 3 inches fell in under 2 hours causing flooding around the County.  Several roads became flooded, including Iowa Highway 9 and U.S. Highway 169.  Very heavy rain in the 2 to 4 inch range fell in Hamilton County during a 2 hour period.  This caused considerable flooding in the county, especially over the northwest half.  There was one high wind event.  In what turned out to be a high wind event occurred in Marion County.  A 60 MPH wind was recorded in Pella.  The event was in the wake of the line of thunderstorms and actually effected a several county area with winds of 40 to 50 MPH.  Temperatures shot up 9 degrees in a few minutes at the Des Moines Airport as a 51 MPH wind gust pushed the temperature up to 90 during the mid evening hours.

A nearly stationary frontal boundary extended nearly east to west across the state along U.S. Highway 20, or roughly from Fort Dodge to Waterloo.  Very unstable air was to the south of the front with dew point temperatures in the low to mid 70s common.  By early afternoon, CAPE values were near 5000 J/KG with lifted indices in the -10 to -12 C. range.  A dry line advanced east toward the state along with the passage of a short wave lifting northeast across the area.  Thunderstorms fired along the triple point by the early afternoon hours in northwest Iowa.  The storms became severe very quickly and produced tornadoes as the sounding profile became very favorable.  In addition, significant mid level cooling took place as 700 mb temperatures fell several degrees during the day.   Most of the storms remained over the north third of the state with numerous reports of tornadoes.  The bulk of the tornadoes progressed southeast from northwest Iowa into the central counties of the state as the afternoon turned into evening.  For the most part, the tornadoes were quite small with only a few remaining on the ground for more than a few tenths of a mile.  Two tornadoes in Palo Alto and Emmet Counties were on the ground for a significant period of time, however they tracked over open country.  There were several tornadoes in Webster County.  Most of them were also small and did little damage, however one tornado near Otho hit two farmsteads there causing considerable damage.  One farmstead was nearly destroyed, including significant damage to the house.  Hail was common with the storms with much of it in the three quarter to one and one quarter inch diameter range.  There were a few golf ball size hail reports in Webster and Hamilton Counties, and one tennis ball size hail report in Stratford in Hamilton County.  Spotty reports of high were were received.  Winds were in the 60 to 70 MPH range.  Rainfall became a problem in a couple areas.  In Kossuth County rainfall of 2 to over 3 inches fell in under 2 hours causing flooding around the County.  Several roads became flooded, including Iowa Highway 9 and U.S. Highway 169.  Very heavy rain in the 2 to 4 inch range fell in Hamilton County during a 2 hour period.  This caused considerable flooding in the county, especially over the northwest half.  There was one high wind event.  In what turned out to be a high wind event occurred in Marion County.  A 60 MPH wind was recorded in Pella.  The event was in the wake of the line of thunderstorms and actually effected a several county area with winds of 40 to 50 MPH.  Temperatures shot up 9 degrees in a few minutes at the Des Moines Airport as a 51 MPH wind gust pushed the temperature up to 90 during the mid evening hours.

The front that moved through our area on Wednesday June 9th maintained its identity and began to move north as a warm front during the afternoon of the 13th. The first cell of the day became a long-lived supercell. This storm moved through the Midland and Bay City areas, over the south end of Saginaw Bay, and into Huron county before moving out over the open waters of Lake Huron. Later in the afternoon and during the evening a nearly solid line of storms developed along a north-south surface trough over western lower Michigan. These storms developed bowing characteristics as they moved into southeast Michigan and generated some straight-line wind damage. The Midland Fire Department called out two extra crews to answer about 30 storm-related calls of downed wires, broken utility poles and fallen trees. At least two trees crashed into homes.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tropical airmass was in place over Iowa as a weak cold front moved southeast into the state.  At the same time, a tropical feature lifted north across Texas into Oklahoma and fed moisture into the state.  Dew points south of the front rose into the mid 70s by the late morning hours.  Precipitable water values were in the one and one half to two inch range with CAPE values across the state ranging from 1500 J/kg along the front to 3500 J/kg a ways ahead of the front.  Zero to 3 km CAPE values were between 100 and 175 J/kg.  During the mid morning hours thunderstorms fired up in northwest Iowa as the MCV from the previous nights MCS moved northeast into western Iowa.  The thunderstorms expanded through the morning into the afternoon hours.  Most of the storms were tropical in nature, but did produce pea to marble size hail at many locations.  There were a few reports of hail up to an inch in diameter.  As the event unfolded, a few of the storms produced downburst winds.  Wind gusts were limited to around 60 MPH.  Two barns were blown down in Webster County by the high winds.  The main event was the heavy tropical rainfall.  A band of heavy rainfall extended from west central into north central Iowa.  A band of two to four inch rainfall extended from near Sac City toward Fort Dodge into the Mason City area.  Locally heavier amounts of 4 to 5 inches were received.  Numerous roads were flooded in Webster County with a main bridge into Fort Dodge close due to high water.  Fifteen roads were flooded in Cerro Gordo County.  In Calhoun County, U.S. Highway 20 east of Rockwell City was under water with numerous county roads flooded.  Heavy rainfall in Des Moines caused flash flooding with water flowing over 2 feet deep over U.S. Highway 6 in town.  Nearly two inches of rain fell within a 30 minute period in the area to produce the flash flood.

A strong low level jet moving over a warm front from Northern Missouri into Central Illinois combined with an upper level disturbance to produce thunderstorms across Iowa and Northern Illinois.  As the storms became better organized, they were prolific producers of hail from 0.75 to 1 inch.  In Muscatine County Iowa, the storms organized into a small bow echo that moved through Rock Island, Henry, Bureau, and Putnam counties in Illinois.  Southern Henry County Illinois took the brunt of the bow echo with near continuous damage from Interstate 74 to Galva, Illinois with the worst damage in Galva.	A second round of thunderstorms developed around dawn from boundaries left over from the overnight storms.  Due to a drier atmosphere, the hail produced by this round of storms was much larger.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 30th, a warm front was draped across eastern Kentucky.  With extremely moist and unstable air, this boundary helped spark the beginning of a most unusual event for eastern Kentucky, and for that matter, for the country.  Countless supercell thunderstorms developed along this boundary for hours on end, causing widespread tree damage and damage to structures.  Flash flooding was also occurring with these storms which contained torrential rain.  Unfortunately for eastern Kentucky, this was not the end to the severe weather or the flooding.  Later in the night, mostly in the early hours of May 31st, a potent cold front burst through, bringing destruction to most if not all eastern Kentucky counties.  Also, so much rain had fallen from the previous afternoon and evening, coupled with more heavy rain during the morning of May 31st, that widespread aerial flooding occurred.  For some counties, as was the case for Estill and Powell Counties, the aerial flooding lasted for days.  The cost of these storms totaled easily in the millions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Clusters of thunderstorms with heavy rains generated WSR-88D Doppler Radar rainfall estimates of 5 to 6 inches within 4 to 6 hours in  Cambria (Columbia Co.), resulting in flash flooding.  Further east, Randolph (Dodge Co.) was hit with a flash flood after torrential rainfalls (unofficial) of 8.6 inches fell during the evening hours of June 9th, followed by another 2.20 inches overnight.  Interestingly, Randolph picked up 13.6 inches of rain in May, 2004, and 13 inches in June, 2004.  Between May 7, 2004 and June 11, 2004, this city measured 25.60 inches of rain (normal for the entire year is bout 33 inches).  Randolph sits a large bowl-shaped depression that has no outside drainage, which applified the flooding problem.  The flash flood in Randolph flooded at least 300 homes, in some cases up to the 1st-floor windows.  At least 15 homes had major flood damage, and 24 businesses were damaged.  Numerous families were evacuated, and flood waters didn't recede until June 12th.         In Cambria, Tarratt Lake on Duck Creek burst through a dam that supported STH 146.  At least half of the road was washed away at that location, resulting in closure of that road for much of the remainder of the summer due to repairs.  Luckily the dam didn't have a complete collapse, and no homes or businesses were damaged.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two rounds of severe weather affected parts of south-central and southeast Wisconsin on June 23rd, with the second round featuring 8 tornadoes, large hail (up to golf-ball size), and powerful straight-line downburst winds.  A warm front moving north through the area resulted in favorable vertical wind shear to allow for supercell development.The 1st round of severe weather was due to a broken line of intense thunderstorms moving  across Walworth, Milwaukee, Racine and Kenosha counties.  Hail of up to 1 inch in diameter and torrential rainfall accompanied these storms before they moved over Lake Michigan and weakened.  The 2nd round of severe weather was dominated by 2 cyclic supercells - one moved east/southeast through Marquette, Green Lake, Fond du Lac, and Washington Counties, spinning up 5 separate tornadoes, dumping hail stones up to 3 inches in diameter, and hurricane-force downburst winds.  The large hail dented several vehicles.  Two of these were rated F3.  Refer to the individual tornado reports for more details.  A more southerly supercell tracked across extreme southern Sauk County and then made a partial right turn and headed southeast through Dane County, spinning up 2 tornadoes in the process, as well as large hail and downburst winds.  One powerful downburst wind in Madison (Dane Co.) blew equipment off the roof of a business at the Midvale Shopping Mall.  A semi southwest of Ft. Atkinson was blown over by straight-line wind gusts.  This southern supercell eventually spun up another tornado in south-central Jefferson County which moved into north-central Walworth County.  Refer to the individual tornado reports for more details.Both supercells had downbursts that generated large hail and powerful, hurricane-force winds north and south of their tracks.  Over all of Wisconsin, 16 tornadoes were documented on June 23rd, which is the 4th highest single-day total (record is 24 on May 8, 1988).  For south-central and southeast Wisconsin, the 8 tornadoes on June 23rd was tied for the 4th highest single-day total (record is 11 on May 8, 1988).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two major rainfall events during the last 10 days of May 2004 resulted in major to near record flooding across parts of East Central and Northeast Iowa that continued into June 2004.  Following is an edited write up from the Service Hydrologist:The first event occurred from the 21st through the 24th, with the hardest hit areas mainly along and north of Interstate 80.  Reported rainfall was as high as 4 inches (Cedar Rapids) during this period, while some locations received 5 to 6 inches.   The high amounts of water from smaller creeks and streams led to rapid rises on the area's larger rivers and streams, then major to near record flooding.  Most of the hardest hit counties, flood-wise, were along the U.S. Highway 20 corridor in Iowa.  In Manchester, Iowa, the Maquoketa River reached its second highest level ever, second only to a crest in the 1950s.  Flooding closed the major east-west road through the city.  That road is also a state highway.  The high water also forced evacuations of some businesses.  Some homes were affected, too.Independence, Iowa also encountered major flooding on the Wapsipinicon River.  Its crest was the sixth highest on record.  Many homes were affected, and the high water forced the evacuation of some businesses in town just like in Manchester.  In Independence, some normally small creeks became major waterways during and after the heavy rain, which flooded some houses and businesses that were some distance from those houses that were affected by high water on the Wapsipinicon River.  High water forced the closing of Iowa Highway 150 on the south side of town, where the road crosses the river.  With this major road shut down, access to the city was inconvenient from the south.  It required one to either travel several miles east on U.S. Highway 20, then back the same several miles to Independence, or to travel west a little and then take a road into the west side of Independence.Jones County, Iowa, also experienced problems from high water on the Wapsipinicon River.  The river in Anamosa crested at the second highest level on record.  The flood fight in Anamosa was successful in keeping most of the city safe from flooding.The second major rain event of the month occurred from the 29th through the 31st.  Reported rainfall was as much as two and a half inches of rain with other locations reporting as much as 3 to 4 inches.  This additional rain led to additional rises and crests on some rivers, with most of the crests occurring in June.  The second crests were in some cases the same as or higher than the first crests.  Lower sections of the Wapsipinicon River, for example, in Clinton and Scott counties, experienced high second crests.  Large amounts of water coming downstream from the first heavy rain event combined with runoff from the second rain event to produce the second highest crest on record on the Wapsipinicon River near De Witt, Iowa.  The high water forced the closing of Old U.S. Highway 61 south of De Witt, Iowa, along with the closing of a business along the river by the highway.  The present U.S. Highway 61-a vital link between northern Scott County, Iowa, and Clinton County, Iowa-was unaffected.The Rock, Pecatonica, and La Moine rivers in Illinois also experienced flooding due to the heavy rains.  Minor flooding occurred on the Rock River while moderate flooding occurred on the Pecatonica River.  The La Moine River experienced minor flooding.The large amounts of water from the tributary rivers in Iowa and Illinois led to rises on the Mississippi River.  Although the entire river rose in response to the large amounts of water, the river rose above flood stage from Lock and Dam15 in the Quad Cities to Gregory Landing, Missouri.  Most of the rest of the crests occurred in June.  The Mississippi River in the Quad Cities did crest during May, however, and it crested just over flood stage.  Only minor flooding resulted.

Moist and unstable air along a stalled frontal boundary set the stage for supercell thunderstorm development during the afternoon and evening hours.  This was round number two for the day.  Numerous supercells developed across southern Wisconsin by the late afternoon hours, which produced three tornadoes, numerous funnel clouds, several large hail reports, and heavy rains.  Funnel cloud reports were collected from Columbia, Dane, Rock, Dodge, and Waukesha counties between 1720 CST and 1913 CST.  The first tornado spun up 3.3 miles east-southeast of Stoughton (Dane Co.), the second tornado spun up 1.2 miles southeast of De Forest (Dane Co.), and the third tornado spun up 2 miles southwest of Fall River (Columbia Co.).  All three tornadoes had no damage associated with them and were all classified as F0s (for detailed path lengths, path widths, and spin up and dissipating points, please consult details above).  In addition to tornadoes, funnel clouds, and large hail, these storms produced heavy rain.  Urban flooding resulted across Ozaukee County after storms produced 1.25 inches of rain in only a 30 minute period.  A few roads were closed and gravel washouts were common.  Refer to several flood and flash flood events for May 23rd, 24th, and 25th, for related information.

An active and very complicated round of severe thunderstorms affected west Texas during the late afternoon and evening of the 5th. Severe weather development was focused in two areas of the region. Convective initiation occurred first near a sub-synoptic scale outflow boundary that was situated across the southeast Permian Basin. This feature was a remnant from overnight convection to the northeast of the area. Two supercell thunderstorms developed along the boundary over rural areas of southeast Midland and northern Upton Counties. As these storms moved east, storm-scale outflow boundaries were observed in local warning radar base reflectivity and velocity data arcing away from the storms toward the west. Both of these boundaries interacted with the larger scale baroclinic boundary under a field of strongly growing convective towers over southern and central Midland County and northeast Crane County. A series of at least four landspout tornadoes were observed as these interactions occurred.The mesoscale boundary began propagating west-northwest across the basin as the supercell storms provided convective enhancement to the cool (east) side of the boundary. Meanwhile strong to severe thunderstorms began propagating east from the mountainous areas of southeast New Mexico and southwest Texas. The convectively enhanced outflow boundary interacted with the complex of storms over the Upper Trans Pecos region. Large hail and two tornadoes were observed in east-central Reeves County.

A very unstable situation took shape over Iowa during the day on the 11th.  A nearly stationary frontal boundary extended nearly east to west across the state along U.S. Highway 20, or roughly from Fort Dodge to Waterloo.  Very unstable air was to the south of the front with dew point temperatures in the low to mid 70s common.  By early afternoon, CAPE values were near 5000 J/KG with lifted indices in the -10 to -12 C. range.  A dry line advanced east toward the state along with the passage of a short wave lifting northeast across the area.  Thunderstorms fired along the triple point by the early afternoon hours in northwest Iowa.  The storms became severe very quickly and produced tornadoes as the sounding profile became very favorable.  In addition, significant mid level cooling took place as 700 mb temperatures fell several degrees during the day.   Most of the storms remained over the north third of the state with numerous reports of tornadoes.  The bulk of the tornadoes progressed southeast from northwest Iowa into the central counties of the state as the afternoon turned into evening.  For the most part, the tornadoes were quite small with only a few remaining on the ground for more than a few tenths of a mile.  Two tornadoes in Palo Alto and Emmet Counties were on the ground for a significant period of time, however they tracked over open country.  There were several tornadoes in Webster County.  Most of them were also small and did little damage, however one tornado near Otho hit two farmsteads there causing considerable damage.  One farmstead was nearly destroyed, including significant damage to the house.  Hail was common with the storms with much of it in the three quarter to one and one quarter inch diameter range.  There were a few golf ball size hail reports in Webster and Hamilton Counties, and one tennis ball size hail report in Stratford in Hamilton County.  Spotty reports of high were were received.  Winds were in the 60 to 70 MPH range.  Rainfall became a problem in a couple areas.  In Kossuth County rainfall of 2 to over 3 inches fell in under 2 hours causing flooding around the County.  Several roads became flooded, including Iowa Highway 9 and U.S. Highway 169.  Very heavy rain in the 2 to 4 inch range fell in Hamilton County during a 2 hour period.  This caused considerable flooding in the county, especially over the northwest half.  There was one high wind event.  In what turned out to be a high wind event occurred in Marion County.  A 60 MPH wind was recorded in Pella.  The event was in the wake of the line of thunderstorms and actually effected a several county area with winds of 40 to 50 MPH.  Temperatures shot up 9 degrees in a few minutes at the Des Moines Airport as a 51 MPH wind gust pushed the temperature up to 90 during the mid evening hours.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 30th, a warm front was draped across eastern Kentucky.  With extremely moist and unstable air, this boundary helped spark the beginning of a most unusual event for eastern Kentucky, and for that matter, for the country.  Countless supercell thunderstorms developed along this boundary for hours on end, causing widespread tree damage and damage to structures.  Flash flooding was also occurring with these storms which contained torrential rain.  Unfortunately for eastern Kentucky, this was not the end to the severe weather or the flooding.  Later in the night, mostly in the early hours of May 31st, a potent cold front burst through, bringing destruction to most if not all eastern Kentucky counties.  Also, so much rain had fallen from the previous afternoon and evening, coupled with more heavy rain during the morning of May 31st, that widespread aerial flooding occurred.  For some counties, as was the case for Estill and Powell Counties, the aerial flooding lasted for days.  The cost of these storms totaled easily in the millions.
